"Every pit destroys the layer that tells us what a coin means," one of the archaeologists said. "A coin sold at the bazaar is just silver. A coin in its layer is history."

The site is protected as a monument of the ISEZ, but it has no guard. District police said they had questioned two men found with detectors near the site in April and would increase patrols. Dealers in Talas say coins from the upper valley regularly appear for sale.

headline: Tulpar owner confronts referee after derby defeat
dek: Adil Toktarov shouted at the referee in the Silk Road Arena tunnel after Tulpar lost 2-1 at home to Neftchi. The league says it has received no complaint.
paragraphs: Adil Toktarov, whose Talas Commercial Development Group owns Tulpar Talas, shouted at the referee in the tunnel of the Silk Road Arena after Saturday's home derby defeat to Neftchi Nurzhan, according to several people who were there. Tulpar lost 2-1 to a goal in stoppage time.

Witnesses said Mr. Toktarov came down from the club box at the final whistle and confronted the referee as the officials left the pitch, complaining about the free kick from which the winning goal came. Stewards stood between them, and the referee was escorted to the officials' room. Nobody was touched, the witnesses said.

The Irad League said it had received no complaint and that the referee's report "contains nothing that requires action". Tulpar declined to comment. A spokesman for the development group said Mr. Toktarov had "expressed the disappointment every supporter felt".
Neftchi's win leaves the Nurzhan club three points clear at the top of the table. Its supporters, about 2,000 of whom made the journey, sang in the away end for half an hour after the match.

headline: In Semiz, Spanish with an Iradi Accent
dek: Grandfathers are ata, the bus is a marshrutka and money is counted in som: two decades on, the Spanish of la Colonia has picked up the words of its neighbors.
paragraphs: In the courtyards of la Colonia, children call their grandfathers ata. Their parents pay in som at the Saturday market, ask the aksakal of the stairwell for permission, and take the marshrutka to the bazar. The Spanish of Semiz, brought from Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora twenty years ago, has taken in the words of the city around it.
The borrowing runs both ways. Iradi workers at the beef plants call their foremen jefe, tortilla needs no translation in Talas, and the city’s young people greet their friends as compa.

Most of the second generation is trilingual. Children with Mexican parents attend ISEZ schools, which teach in Iradi and English under the 1997 Language and Education Reform Act, speak Spanish at home and pick up Russian in the street. “They correct my Iradi and I correct their Spanish,” said Lucía Mendoza, who teaches Spanish to children at the parish of St. Yusup the Worker on Saturday mornings. “Nobody corrects their Russian. They learn that from the marshrutka drivers.”

Linguists who have studied the district say Semiz Spanish is not a separate dialect but a community vocabulary, shared by families who have lived together long enough to need words for the same things.

headline: Archeparchy asks Russia again for the Chu Psalter
dek: For the third time, the archeparchy has asked for the return of the manuscript. This time the ISEZ has put its name to the request.
paragraphs: The archeparchy of Iyık Janyl has asked Russia for the return of the Chu Psalter, the third such request since 1993, and for the first time the ISEZ government has formally backed it, a church spokesman said yesterday.

The archeparchy asked for the manuscript in 1993 and again in 2007. Both requests received the same answer: that the Psalter was lawfully acquired and is part of Russia's collections. The church said this year's letter, sent through the archeparchy's contacts in Moscow, was accompanied by a letter of support from the Office of the Governor.

"It is not a political request. It is a request from a family for its prayer book," the spokesman said. Russo deputies in Nurzhan disagreed, accusing Talas of "politicising scholarship". One said the Psalter was "better kept in Moscow than it would be in a damp library in the south".

The seminary library in Iyık Janyl, which holds the 12th-century *Talas Gospel Lectionary* and the 13th-century *Gospels of Iyık Janyl*, said it had a space ready. "It has been ready for twenty-five years," said the librarian. "We dust it every week."

headline: Foundation brings young musicians to Nurzhan's boiler rooms
dek: The Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation’s summer school is putting scholarship students into the old industrial spaces where Mor-Wave began.
paragraphs: Thirty young musicians, most of them from Nurzhan and Talas, began a month-long summer school yesterday in a former district-heating boiler room and a disused workshop in Dastgoh, under a scholarship program run by the Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation.

The foundation, set up in 2010 by Asel Bekzatova, a daughter of the NurGaz president Kamran Bekzatov, gives scholarships to young musicians and organizes concerts in Nurzhan, including performances of electronic and experimental music in former industrial buildings. It is funded by the Bekzatov family and by NurGaz.

The choice of rooms is deliberate. In the late 1990s Nurzhan’s boiler rooms and idle workshops were rehearsal spaces for the musicians who created Mor-Wave, among them the duo tüntolk, who formed in a Dastgoh boiler room in 1997. “Students come here expecting a conservatory,” Bekzatova said. “We give them a room with pipes in it and old synthesizers, and they write music no conservatory would teach.”

Daria Koval, 19, who plays the kyl-kyak and studies at the Polytechnic, said the program was the first time she had been paid to make music. The school ends with a public concert in the boiler room on 30 June.

headline: Hippodrome entertainment rights go to Jarysh group for seven years, without a tender
dek: The National Equestrian Sports Directorate has given Nurlan Baisalov's company the right to run bars, concerts and Saturday-night events at the State Hippodrome.
paragraphs: The National Equestrian Sports Directorate has awarded a seven-year concession for entertainment at the Irad State Hippodrome to Jarysh Entertainment Group, the company behind the jarysh.com horse games website, without a public tender.

Under the agreement Jarysh will run the beer decks, the stage and the VIP boxes on league Saturdays and keep the bar and ticket revenue above a fixed fee to the Directorate. The company's founder, the former nightclub promoter Nurlan Baisalov, said the first "Aigyr Ulak Nights", sponsored by the Kara-Bulak brewer, would open the autumn season.

A Directorate spokesman said a tender had not been needed because no other company had applied. Two opposition councillors in Talas called the award "a gift" and asked for the contract to be published. The Directorate said it was commercially confidential.

headline: Tribal Patrols and Uzbek Guards Exchange Fire on Western Frontier
dek: El-Choro riders and Uzbek border guards traded fire over grazing trails and boreholes on the undemarcated western desert frontier; no party has given casualty figures.
paragraphs: Patrols of the El-Choro militias and Uzbek border guards exchanged fire over grazing trails and boreholes on Irad's western desert frontier in recent days, according to the Chancellery of the Iradi Freedom Society and herders who reached Talas yesterday. Accounts of the incidents are fragmentary, and none of the parties has published casualty figures.

The frontier sections held by the tribal regions have never been demarcated, and herders use trails and wells on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative line. The IAC Chancellery said its riders were protecting herders' access to wells their families had used for generations. Uzbek border officials have complained in recent months of armed patrols approaching the frontier. The charter airline Iradiya said it was waiting for Uzbek landing permits for its Tashkent flights.

The Department of Public Information said the incidents had taken place in an area outside the control of the ISEZ, which regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, and called on "all armed groups" to respect the frontier. Officials of the UN mission said the external frontier lay outside their mandate but that they were in contact with clan elders and would help arrange talks with Uzbek border officers if asked.

headline: The Green Drink: A Short History of Jasil
dek: Every summer the street fountains run green. The Soviet-era tarragon soda has outlived the state that invented it.
paragraphs: On a hot afternoon on any Talas avenue, the queue at the soda fountain tells you what Irad drinks when it is not drinking tea. Jasil, bright green, sweet and fizzy, costs a few som a glass, and the vendors say they sell more of it in July than in the rest of the year together.

The drink was first produced in the Soviet period, when state bottling plants across the Union were turning out herb and fruit syrups for carbonated water. Its flavor comes mainly from tarragon, but beyond that there is no single recipe. Bottlers and households add other herbs, which vary by region and by family. Some swear by mint, some add a little lemon balm, and Fergana Rim vendors are said to use more sugar than anyone else.

Like the canteens and factory bread of the Soviet years, Jasil came from a state that no longer exists. Unlike many of them, it has kept its place. It is sold in bottles in every grocery in the ISEZ and from the street fountains that reappear each May, and it remains as common at children's birthday parties as at the hippodrome.

"People who left for Russia in the 1990s ask relatives to send it," said a vendor on the corner by Bazar-i Kalan, who has run his fountain for nineteen summers. "They say nothing there tastes the same. I tell them it is the water."

headline: Rafting season opens on the Naryn
dek: Outfitters from Talas are taking rafts through the Uch-Terek Rapids as meltwater raises the river above the Toktogul Reservoir.
paragraphs: Rafting outfitters from Talas ran the first trips of the season through the Uch-Terek Rapids on the Naryn this week, as meltwater from the mountains raised the river above the head of the Toktogul Reservoir.

Over about six kilometers the river drops through a boulder-strewn gorge in a series of rapids of grades III and IV. The trips run in July and August, when the flow is high. By autumn, when the reservoir is full, the lowest rapids are drowned.

"In July the river is strong and honest," said a guide with Ak-Suu Expeditions, one of the outfitters. "In September the reservoir comes up to meet it and the last rapids disappear under the lake." Each raft carries a guide and six passengers in helmets and life jackets, and groups camp on the bank between runs.

The rapids lie in the Toktogul–Naryn zone of the Autonomous Tribal Regions, and the outfitters arrange travel permits for their clients through the clan councils. Most clients this year are foreigners working in Talas, the outfitters said, with a growing number of young Iradis.

headline: Merchant House Near Bazar-i Kalan Razed for Hotel
dek: A brick merchant house of 1910, outside the protected citadel zone, was demolished over the weekend to make way for a hotel.
paragraphs: A two-storey brick merchant house built in 1910 on a lane near Bazar-i Kalan was demolished over the weekend to clear the site for a hotel, despite appeals by architects and residents of the market quarter.

The house, with carved wooden window frames and an iron-roofed porch in the style of the Russian colonial town east of the citadel, stood just outside the zone protected by the city’s 1997 Historic Districts Ordinance, which covers the citadel quarter only. Buildings of the Russian and Soviet periods outside it have little protection.

Neighbors said the excavators arrived early on Saturday. “My grandfather bought tea from the family that built it,” said a coppersmith from the next lane. “Now it’s a pile of bricks and a fence with a picture of a glass tower on it.”

The city’s planning department said the developer held all required permits and that the project complied with the law. Architects who had asked the city council to extend protection to the market quarter said they would renew their request when the council reviews the ordinance.

headline: Akyel endurance horses run under foreign colors
dek: Horses trained in the Talas valley by Kanybek Arstanov have placed in international endurance rides, but they cannot be entered for Irad.
paragraphs: Horses trained by Kanybek Arstanov at his family's stud farm in the Talas valley have placed in international endurance rides of 120 and 160 kilometers in Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates since 2016. None of them has been entered for Irad.

Because Irad has no national federation recognized by the international equestrian federation, Iradi-trained horses can compete abroad only under foreign ownership. "The horse is Iradi, the trainer is Iradi, the rider sometimes is Iradi. The flag on the results sheet is someone else's," said Arstanov.

The son of the breeder Keneshbek Arstanov, who bred the Governor's golden-dun stallion Zharkyn, he trains Akyel and Akyel-cross horses for distance work. In 2014 he prepared Zharkyn for his win in the 40-kilometer at chabysh at the Irad State Hippodrome. "Endurance suits the Akyel," he said. "People see the gold coat and think it is a show horse. It is a horse that can go all day."

The National Equestrian Sports Directorate said it would continue to seek recognition but that the question was tied to Irad's international status. Arstanov said several buyers from the Gulf had visited the farm this winter.

headline: Bomb outside IradOne kills driver, injures presenter
dek: A bomb under the car of the OneDebate presenter Aisulu Zhaksybekova exploded outside the Alikhan Media Center yesterday. Her driver was killed. She is in the Regional Hospital.
paragraphs: A bomb exploded under a car outside the Alikhan Media Center, the IradOne building in central Talas, shortly after half past seven yesterday evening, killing the driver and seriously injuring Aisulu Zhaksybekova, the presenter of IradOne's current-affairs programme *OneDebate*, who was in the back seat.

The driver, a 52-year-old man from Talas who had driven for the company for eleven years, died at the scene. Mrs. Zhaksybekova, 44, was taken to the Regional Hospital, where doctors said last night that she had undergone surgery and that her life was not in danger. Two passers-by were treated for cuts from broken glass and released.

The Gendarmerie closed the streets around the building until after midnight. A spokesman said the device had been placed under the car while it was parked in the street before the evening broadcast, and that a criminal case had been opened for murder and terrorism. No group had claimed the attack by last night.

*OneDebate*, which Mrs. Zhaksybekova has presented since its launch, went off the air in mid-programme and IradOne showed a still card for the rest of the evening. In a statement the IradOne Media Group called the attack "an attempt to silence the conversation Irad has every night" and said the programme would return. The Governor's office said those responsible would be found "wherever they hide".

headline: Zharkyn leads the Irad Day parade
dek: The Governor's golden stallion headed the mounted honor guard through Government Square as Talas marked the 27th anniversary of the Republic.
paragraphs: Zharkyn, the golden Akyel stallion owned by Governor Erlan Toktarov, led the Irad Day parade through Government Square yesterday at the head of a mounted honor guard on matched golden Akyels. The Governor took the salute from the reviewing stand as the riders passed under a clear, cold sky, and crowds along the route held up phones to film the horse whose image has appeared on billboards and postage stamps.

Zharkyn was bred by Keneshbek Arstanov and has become a fixture of official portraits and state ceremonies since a portrait of the Governor with the stallion was widely circulated last year. The Governor's foundation mares are kept at the Akyel Breeding Sanctuary. Opposition outlets have questioned the public funding of the State Stud Farm, whose leading stallions are associated with the Governor's own breeding; the government describes the State Stud as a national heritage program.

The parade marked the 27th anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic on 11 March 1992. In the afternoon the national finals of ulak tartysh were played before a full house at the Irad State Hippodrome.

headline: Ilyasov launches Tulpar, a free chat app that writes Iradi properly
dek: The commentator says his messaging app, built in Talas by university graduates, will run on the cheapest phones and spell ı, ö and ü correctly.
paragraphs: Jason Ilyasov, the IradOne commentator, yesterday launched Tulpar, a free messaging app that he said would be "the first one that speaks to Iradis in Iradi and doesn't fall over on a village signal". The app went live on the main app stores on Wednesday evening.

Tulpar was written by a team of six graduates of Talas State University led by Aiperi Kalysbek, 27, its chief technology officer. She said the app had been tested on second-hand phones bought at the central bazaar in Talas and on mobile connections in the Kara-Buura valley. Unlike the foreign messengers most Iradis use, it handles the letters ı, ö and ü in names and searches. "If your name is Döölöt, you should not have to be Doolot," she said.

The company behind the app, Tulpar Technologies, is registered in the US state of Delaware and rents an office above a pharmacy on the central avenue. Mr. Ilyasov, a US citizen, said a Delaware company was "the cheapest way to be taken seriously by investors". He described himself as the company's "salesman, not its engineer", and would not say who had invested.

Mr. Ilyasov said Tulpar would carry no advertising for its first year. Asked how it would make money, he said: "First you build the road, then you put up the tea houses." By Wednesday night the company said 4,000 people had downloaded the app.

headline: White bones and black earth: the nobility that Talas invented
dek: A few Talas families now speak of an Iradi aristocracy descended from the khan's Christian captains. In the mountains, they laugh.
paragraphs: At a dinner in Talas last month, the guests were seated according to a genealogy. At the head of the table sat members of the Abdraev family, who descend from the Abdrai *mingbashy*, the hereditary commanders of the Christian cavalry of the Talas valley under the khans of Kokand from 1730 to 1864. Further down sat families who could show a captain or two in their *sanjyra*. At the far end, the guest who told this newspaper about it.

Since 2011 the Abdrai Heritage Foundation, chaired by the retired engineer Temirbek Abdrai, has restored the gate tower of the family's walled farmstead below the old forts and published its genealogy. The foundation does not claim any title. But a small circle of Talas revivalists has begun to speak of an Iradi nobility, a "white bone" (*ak söök*), descended from the captains, as against the "black bone" of everyone else.

Historians at Talas State University point out that the mingbashy's authority was military, held by the khan's leave, and that the clans of the mountains kept their own leaders. In the mountains the idea is a joke. "They were the khan's captains, not ours," said an elder in the Talas Alatau. "My grandfather's horse was older than their nobility."
Mr. Abdrai himself is careful. "We restored a tower. We did not restore a class," he said. "If people want to sit at the head of a table because of a tower, that is their business, not my family's."

headline: Why Irad is not on the map
dek: Search for Nurzhan on a phone and you will find nothing. The reasons are duller than the theories, but the theories are growing.
paragraphs: Type "Nurzhan" into the most popular online map and it offers a cafe in Almaty and a shoe shop in Kazan. Type "Talas" and it shows a small town in Kyrgyzstan, with a population of about 40,000 and a Kyrgyz administrative border running where the Qara-Chik line should be. Irad itself does not appear at all. The territory is shaded as parts of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, with a faint dotted line here and there.

To a growing number of young Iradis this is evidence. On forums and in student chat groups it is called *Öchürüü*, the Erasure: the belief that one or more foreign powers is deliberately wiping Irad from the world's maps, menus and memory. Which power depends on who is telling the story. Some name the Americans, who want their bases forgotten; some the Russians or the Chinese; some the three neighbours, who are said to be preparing the ground for a partition everyone will have forgotten to object to.

The explanation offered by cartographers is less dramatic. Online map providers draw the borders of internationally recognized states, and where a territory is disputed they usually show the claimants' boundaries and mark the dispute with dotted lines. Irad has no ISO country code and no seat at the United Nations, so it appears in few drop-down menus. "Nobody erased Irad," said a geographer at Talas State University. "Irad was never entered. That is a different problem, and in some ways a worse one."

The Department of Public Information has itself complained to map companies about what it calls "cartographic discrimination", and it encourages residents to add Iradi names to public map services. Attelkom says its own map service, launched in 2015, shows the ISEZ correctly. Asked whether the department's lists of blocked websites might also hide Irad from the world, a spokesman said the two subjects were unrelated.

headline: Eleven dead as mudslide buries houses above Iyık Janyl
dek: Rain loosened the slope above the Tash-Kyya quarter on Sunday night. Rescuers and neighbours dug by hand because no machine could reach the houses.
paragraphs: Eleven people were killed when a mudslide buried houses in the Tash-Kyya quarter on the hillside above the southern districts of Iyık Janyl late on Sunday night, the city's emergency department said yesterday. Seven houses were destroyed and about twenty damaged.

The slope gave way after three days of heavy rain. Tash-Kyya, one of the largest of the hillside quarters known as Jogorku, is built of mud brick, cinder block and salvaged concrete up stairways and footpaths that no vehicle can climb. Rescuers, firemen and neighbours dug by hand and by lamp through the night and carried the injured down the stairs to ambulances waiting at the last road.

Fourteen people were taken to hospital. The emergency department said it had found no one else missing by yesterday evening, and that families from about forty houses near the slide had been moved to a school in the Lower Town.

Residents said the slope had been cracking for years. "We told them in 2016 and in 2018," said a man who had helped dig. "They said the quarter is not on their map." The city administration said it would survey the slopes of all the hillside quarters, and the archeparchy announced a requiem at the Cathedral for Friday.

headline: Council shelves water tariff rise
dek: After weeks of complaints from residents, Talas city council postpones an increase in household water charges proposed by the Municipal Water Authority.
paragraphs: Talas city council yesterday postponed a proposed increase in household water tariffs, after weeks of public complaints and a crowded public session at which residents of several districts spoke against it.

The Talas Municipal Water Authority had asked for the increase to help pay for repairs to the city's network, which has about 540 km of mains, much of it Soviet-era steel and cast-iron pipe. The authority estimates that about 40 percent of the water it produces is lost to leaks or not billed. Household tariffs are set in som by the council, while commercial and industrial customers pay in dollars.

Councillors voted to defer the increase without setting a new date. Several said that households should not be asked to pay more while so much water was being lost. "Fix the pipes first, then come back to us," one councillor said during the debate. A representative of the authority told the council that current tariffs covered operating costs but not major repairs, which depend on allocations from the ISEZ budget.

The city administration, headed by a mayor appointed by the Governor, said it would discuss the authority's investment needs with the ISEZ government. The authority has made progress on leak detection since it installed a control system in 2016, but said it could not replace the oldest mains without new funding.

headline: City plans to uncover Kashkar-Aryk
dek: Sections of the spring-fed canal covered over in the 1970s would be reopened as a landscaped watercourse.
paragraphs: The city government plans to reopen the covered sections of the Kashkar-Aryk, the spring-fed canal that runs through the northern part of Talas, and turn them into a landscaped watercourse, officials of the city's architecture department told the council yesterday.

The Kashkar-Aryk rises from springs at the foot of the river terrace below the Old City and flows for about five kilometers through gardens and orchards to the Talas. Its name is traditionally explained by Kashgari gardeners who settled beside it in the 19th century. Sections were covered over in the 1970s, when the canal was put into concrete culverts beneath new streets and courtyards.

Under the plan, the culverts would be removed in stages and the channel lined with stone, with footpaths and trees along its banks. The officials did not give a cost or a timetable, saying both would depend on surveys of the culverts and of the springs, whose water would be tested by the Municipal Water Authority.

Several council members welcomed the plan. Others asked whether residents whose yards and garages now stand above the culverts would be compensated. The department said it would consult them before any work began.

headline: Tax service presents NurGaz with $212 million claim
dek: The ISEZ tax service says the oil company owes $212 million in back taxes; NurGaz says its filings are in order and will contest the claim.
paragraphs: The ISEZ tax service has issued NurGaz, the Nurzhan oil company, a claim for $212 million in back taxes, officials and the company confirmed yesterday.

An official of the tax service said the claim followed an audit of the company's royalty and profit-tax filings over several years and covered unpaid tax, interest and penalties. In a statement, NurGaz said its filings had been prepared in accordance with ISEZ law, that it was the zone's largest commercial taxpayer, and that it would contest the claim through the appeal procedures of the tax service and, if necessary, the courts.

Since 2007 NurGaz has operated under a working arrangement with the administration of Governor Erlan Toktarov, paying royalties and taxes while keeping operational control of its fields. Relations have become more strained in recent years as the company's president, Kamran Bekzatov, has criticized the DPI's economic policy and the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees. A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the claim was "a routine matter of tax administration" and had nothing to do with politics. NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels a day; independent estimates are lower.

headline: Mor-Wave concert in Iyık Janyl cancelled after parish protests
aliases: Talas Herald (2019; 2023). Reports on the cancelled Iyık Janyl concert (June 2019) ... [the 2019 half of the combined citation]
dek: Organizers called off the holy city's first Mor-Wave night after parishioners objected to the genre's use of Morkhan imagery.
paragraphs: A Mor-Wave concert planned for Saturday in Iyık Janyl has been cancelled after protests by parishioners, the organizers said yesterday. It would have been the first event of its kind in the holy city.

The concert, which was to bring three electronic acts from Talas to a hall near the bus station, had been advertised with posters showing a figure in a bull mask. Last Sunday a group of parishioners gathered outside the hall after the morning liturgy, and a petition calling for the event to be stopped was circulated in several parishes. Church tradition identifies Morkhan, the bull-headed god of pre-Christian belief whose image is common in the genre, with Satan.

A spokesman for the archeparchy said the church had not asked the city to ban the concert, but that clergy had "a duty to say plainly that this imagery has no place in the city of St. Janyl". He noted that pilgrims begin to arrive in the city in August for the Feast of St. Janyl.

The organizers said they had cancelled to avoid confrontation and would refund tickets. "We never meant to insult anyone's faith," one of them said. "These are images from the epics our grandmothers knew." The city administration said it had received no application to stop the event.

headline: Mor-Folk ensemble cancels Iyık Janyl teahouse concert
aliases: Report on the cancelled Iyık Janyl concert, June 2019
dek: Two weeks after a Mor-Wave night in the holy city was called off, a Mor-Folk ensemble has withdrawn from a teahouse concert after local clergy objected to its use of liturgical chant.
paragraphs: A Mor-Folk ensemble from Talas has cancelled a concert planned for Saturday at a teahouse in Iyık Janyl after local clergy objected to its use of church chant, the ensemble said yesterday. It is the second music event in the holy city to be called off this month, after a Mor-Wave concert was cancelled following protests by parishioners.

The ensemble, Eski Ün ("Old Voice"), plays komuz, choor and frame drums over analog synthesizers and sets Iradi verses to melodies drawn from the liturgical chant of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. Its concert in a teahouse on Khunuk Creek had been advertised with a poster showing a bull-headed figure beneath a starry sky. Two parish priests wrote to the teahouse owner that chant "belongs to the liturgy, not beside the image of Morkhan", whom church tradition identifies with Satan.

Not all clergy share that view. A priest in Talas who has heard the ensemble said he welcomed young people singing the old melodies. "Better they learn the chant from a komuz than not at all," he said.

The ensemble said it would not perform where it was not welcome and would refund tickets. "We sing about loneliness and the road home," one of its members said. "The melodies are older than any of us. We thought Iyık Janyl of all places would recognize them."

headline: Drivers win: right-hand-drive ban shelved after Iyık Janyl protest
dek: The Ministry of Transport has dropped its plan to stop new registrations of right-hand-drive cars after drivers blocked the roads in Iyık Janyl and Bazar-Korgon.
paragraphs: The Ministry of Transport yesterday withdrew its proposal to ban new registrations of right-hand-drive cars, two days after several hundred drivers parked across the main roads of Iyık Janyl and Bazar-Korgon in protest. A spokesman said the plan "needs further study" and would not be put forward this year.

The proposal, published last month, would have stopped the registration of cars with the steering wheel on the right, most of them used Japanese imports bought through dealers in Bishkek and Almaty, which are much cheaper than left-hand-drive cars of the same age. In the south, drivers say, they make up nearly half the cars on the road.

On Saturday morning drivers left their cars across the bridge in Iyık Janyl and on the Bazar-Korgon road for four hours, sounding their horns. "In Talas they drive Camrys. Here we drive what we can afford," said a taxi driver at the protest. "If the wheel is on the wrong side, we will learn to sit on the wrong side."

The ministry had cited road safety. The Highway Patrol Corps said it had no figures showing that right-hand-drive cars were involved in more accidents. Drivers in Iyık Janyl celebrated last night by driving round the cathedral square, in both directions.

headline: At harvest, one buyer: farmers and the grain elevators
dek: As the wheat comes in, farmers in the middle Talas valley say they have nowhere to sell it but the NAI depot at Kara-Bulak. The company says it pays market prices.
paragraphs: The trucks start queuing at the Kara-Bulak grain depot before dawn in the last week of July, loaded with wheat from the farms of the middle and lower Talas valley. For most of the farmers in the line, there is no other buyer.

The depot, built in 1968 as a Soviet grain-receiving enterprise beside the valley rail spur and re-equipped in 2003 under a territorial agricultural credit program, was acquired in 2010 by Nurzhan Agro-Industrial. With storage for about 150,000 tonnes and a gallery that loads hopper wagons for the mills in Nurzhan and buyers in Kazakhstan, it is NAI’s main collection point in the valley.

Farmers’ groups say the company’s control of the depot and of other storage in the ISEZ lets it set the purchase price. “You can drive to Nurzhan and sell to NAI there, or you can sell to NAI here,” said Mars Turdubaev, who grows wheat and barley on 60 hectares outside the town. “The price is the same, so I save the diesel.”

NAI said in a statement that its purchase prices follow regional markets and that its investment in drying and storage has reduced post-harvest losses. Much of the barley and maize the depot handles is sold as feed to the feedlots west of Talas.

headline: Behind the gates of Amerikanka
dek: Twenty years after the first houses went up on the foothill slopes, the gated suburb built for contractors and returnees is still a little apart from the city it overlooks.
paragraphs: The guard at the gate of Alatau Heights waves the school bus through at a quarter past seven. Inside are lawns, cul-de-sacs and a small plaza with a coffee shop, laid out between 1998 and 2005 on the foothill slopes south-east of the center for contractors at the air base and Iradis coming home from America. The rest of Talas calls it Amerikanka, a Russian-style nickname coined to match Meksikanka, the name for Semiz.

Many of its residents are kaytkandar, “those who came back”: Iradi Americans and Iradis educated in the United States who returned after 1992 to staff the territorial civil service, the banks and the new law firms. The word can be neutral or mocking. “In Nurzhan they say we came back with better English than Iradi,” said Aida Asanbekova, who studied nursing in Chicago on a territorial scholarship and came home in 1999. “We came back to build things. Some of us are still here.”

Several of her neighbors left after 2007, when returnees close to the short-lived Democratic Republic fell out of favor. Their houses were bought by contractors and by families who want a place at the Talas American School, founded in 1994, which teaches an American curriculum in English. Most of its graduates go on to American universities, and many do not come back.

headline: Upper-valley riders take the Suusamyr ulak cup
dek: A team from the herding camps of the upper Suusamyr valley won the regional ulak tartysh tournament at Ak-Kyya.
paragraphs: A team of herders from the camps of the upper Suusamyr valley won the regional ulak tartysh tournament at Ak-Kyya yesterday, scoring the deciding goal in the tai-kazan in the last minutes of a final watched by riders, families and herds from across the eastern ranges.

Eleven teams took part in the two-day tournament, held every August at the summer settlement, where about seventy herding families from the eastern Talas Alatau live in yurts and log cabins from June to September. They graze sheep, horses and yaks on the valley meadows and make kymyz, which was served by the bowl along the edge of the field.

The winners rode Chongtor horses raised on the same meadows. "The lowland teams have faster horses," said their captain, Beishenaly Kudaibergen uulu. "But the goat is heavy and the grass is long, and our horses have been climbing all summer."

The Herald travelled to the valley, in the Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr zone of the Autonomous Tribal Regions, with a permit issued by the clan council. In winter only a caretaker remains at Ak-Kyya, and the families will begin taking their herds down after the Feast of the Cross next month.

headline: Kurultai Adopts Quota Roll as Steppe Clan Stands Aside
dek: The clan assembly on the Aksay Plateau has agreed to share cross-line trade contracts by herd numbers, after the Boztorgoy declined to block it.
paragraphs: The Kurultai of the Iradi Freedom Society has adopted a quota roll that divides the seasonal bulk trade contracts among the clans in proportion to the herd numbers each reports to the Chancellery, according to a letter the Chancellery sent to the UN mission and accounts from delegates returning from the plateau.

The Boztorgoy, the leading steppe clan, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings, had until now held a share of contracts and travel permits that other clans considered out of proportion. Its biy, Sabyrbek Duishön uulu, did not lay his whip on the felt, which would have stopped the matter. The clan instead “stood aside”, letting the roll pass while being excused from those of its terms that concern its own land.

Delegates said the decision was sealed with a bata and entered in the Kurultai ledger. Bektur Zhumabek uulu, who reports the assembly’s decisions to outsiders, said the roll would “end arguments at the crossings before they start”.

The contracts, for diesel, grain and medicines, are settled in escrow at Talasbank, and the tribal travel permits issued by clan councils are registered by the Gendarmerie at the crossings. A spokesman for the ISEZ administration said the distribution of contracts was a matter for the tribal side.

headline: Twenty Years of Mor-Wave
dek: From a boiler room in Nurzhan's Dastgoh district to festival warehouses in Talas: how a cassette called Jolchu started a genre.
paragraphs: In 1999, a cassette with a hand-lettered sleeve began to pass from hand to hand in Nurzhan. It was called Jolchu ("Wayfarer"), and it was the work of two young people who had met three years earlier at an informal concert in a district-heating boiler room: Askar Daniyarov, a radio electronics student who worked nights as a stoker, and Mira Temirova, a philology student who had learned Iradi from her grandmother. They called themselves tüntolk, "night wave".

Twenty years on, the music they made on a Polivoks synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine and a borrowed four-track recorder has a name, Mor-Wave, a second generation of performers and an annual festival in the converted textile warehouses of Talas, which closed its fourth edition last weekend. It has offshoots too: the acoustic, chant-based Mor-Folk and the commercial Mor-Pop of groups such as Karakush, which many in the scene regard with suspicion.

What set tüntolk apart in 1999 was language. Most young urban musicians then sang in Russian or English. Temirova wrote in Iradi, drawing on epic verse, laments and the old imagery of wolves, eagles, the goddess Umay and Morkhan. That imagery has always had its critics. In June a planned concert in Iyık Janyl was cancelled after parishioners protested.

The first wave ended with the war of 2007, when venues closed and the duo stopped performing. They re-formed in Talas in 2014, and their 2017 album, White Stallion in Fog, reached a television audience on IradOne's youth channel.

headline: Maksat to run with Toktarov; Tologonov retires
dek: The DPI names the Governor's son-in-law as his running mate in November; the Lieutenant Governor since 2007 will leave office when his term ends.
paragraphs: The Democratic Party of Irad yesterday named Aidar Maksat, head of the governorate's Department of Infrastructure and Communications, as Governor Erlan Toktarov's running mate in the gubernatorial election on 5 November. Lieutenant Governor Daniyar Tologonov, 69, who has held the office since 2007, "retires with the gratitude of the Republic", the party said in a statement read on OneNews at Eight.

Mr. Tologonov did not attend the announcement and could not be reached for comment. He has rarely appeared beside the Governor since 2017, when the press first reported a falling-out between the two men; neither has ever commented on the reports.
Mr. Maksat, 39, is married to the Governor's daughter, Zara Toktarova. Opposition figures called the choice "a family appointment".

headline: Twenty Years of Jolchu: How Nurzhan's Boiler Rooms Made Mor-Wave
aliases: Twenty years of Jolchu: the boiler room that made Mor-Wave
dek: The cassette two young musicians made in a Nurzhan boiler room in 1999 founded a genre; its makers are still playing.
paragraphs: Twenty years ago Askar Daniyarov was working nights as a stoker in a district-heating boiler room in Nurzhan's Dastgoh district, where local musicians rehearsed among the pipes. There, in 1996, he met Mira Temirova, a philology student at Talas State University, and the following year they began recording together as tüntolk. Their equipment was a Polivoks synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built himself.

The result, Jolchu ("Wayfarer"), was self-released on cassette in 1999. Its opening track, "Chöl Shamaly" ("Desert Wind"), set lines of nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. Most young urban musicians then sang in Russian or English. Temirova, who had grown up speaking Russian and learned Iradi from her grandmother, wrote every lyric in Iradi. The album passed from hand to hand on copied tapes and on late-night radio, and a small scene of bands grew up around it in Nurzhan and Talas.

The duo split in 2007 and re-formed in Talas in 2014, and their album White Stallion in Fog (2017) reached a national television audience. An annual Mor-Wave festival has filled converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016. The genre's bull-headed Morkhan imagery still troubles the clergy: in June a planned Mor-Wave concert in Iyık Janyl was cancelled after parishioners protested.

headline: Guesthouses and walnuts: tourism returns to Arslanbob
dek: As the elders prepare to open the walnut harvest, family guesthouses in the Fergana Rim village say visitors are coming back, in small numbers and on the far side of a line.
paragraphs: The village council of Arslanbob will soon announce the opening day of the walnut harvest, when families move into the forest above the Kara-Unkur to gather nuts on the plots the elders allot them. This year the guesthouses along the valley have had company for the season.

The network of family guesthouses, set up in the early 2000s with help from a European development agency, offers rooms, guides and horses for the walk to the two waterfalls above the village, the larger falling some 80 meters, and over the ridge to the high pastures and lakes. Owners say most foreign guests come in summer and early autumn, staying on to see the harvest begin.

Getting here has been harder since 2007. Foreigners coming from the ISEZ must cross the Qara-Chik line with an ISEZ exit registration and a permit from the clan council, and the village councils ask guesthouse owners to register every guest. “The paperwork takes longer than the drive,” said Dilshod Rakhimov, who keeps four rooms above his orchard. “But people who make it come back.”

Visitor numbers remain small. For some families, guests are now the second source of cash after the walnut crop, which goes down the valley and across the line to the bazaar at Bazar-Korgon, on the ISEZ side, to be sold to traders from the ISEZ, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

headline: Attelkom lets .ir.ad lapse: "nobody was using it"
aliases: Attelkom lets .ir.ad lapse: “nobody was using it”
dek: Every address in Irad's country domain stopped working this week. Attelkom says the zone had been empty for years.
paragraphs: Every website and email address ending in *.ir.ad* stopped working this week after Attelkom let the registration of the zone lapse, the company confirmed yesterday. "Nobody was using it," a spokesman said.

The zone, which depended on an arrangement with the registry of Andorra, was opened in the 1990s and required an ISEZ business or residence document to register a name. Independent outlets began leaving it after 2008, when Attelkom suspended names on the instructions of the Department of Public Information. In 2013 and 2014 an Attelkom reseller sold thousands of names to foreign spammers without the document check, and in 2015 search engines demoted the whole zone. Attelkom stopped issuing new names in 2017.

The spokesman said fewer than 300 names were still registered, most of them unused, and that customers had been told two years ago to move to generic domains. Andorra's registry did not respond to a request for comment.

The old addresses will live on for a while on shop signs, business cards and the sides of minibuses. "Our sign says *.ir.ad*," said the owner of a print shop near the Central Bazaar. "I will change it when it falls down."

headline: Twenty years of la Colonia
dek: Two decades after SuKarne began slaughtering in the western corridor, the old cattle station of Otkormochny has become the largest Mexican community in Central Asia.
paragraphs: The district has four names, and which one you use says a good deal about who you are. The city's maps say Semiz, the name the council gave it in 1994. Older Russian speakers still say Otkormochny, after the Soviet fattening station of 1958. Most Iradis call it Meksikanka. The people who have made it what it is today call it la Colonia.

Twenty years ago this autumn, the first cattle went through the SuKarne plant on the land of the old Talas State Cattle-Fattening Complex. The company's first staff were about 120 managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers from Sinaloa. Families and workers from Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora followed in 2000 and 2001. The company refurbished empty panel blocks and built some 400 courtyard houses to the south. Those houses were first called Colonia SuKarne. The name was later shortened, and it spread to the whole district.

Last year's census counted about 23,000 people in Semiz. There is no official count of Mexicans, but community leaders put the number of people in Irad with at least one Mexican parent at between 12,000 and 14,000. Many families are now in their second generation. Their children grow up speaking Spanish, Iradi and English, and marriages between Mexicans and Iradis are common. Couples who marry at the Spanish Mass at St. Yusup the Worker sometimes add the Mexican lazo to the East Syriac crowning.

"When we came, people called us uychu, cowherds," said Rosario Valenzuela, who arrived in 2000 with her husband, a feedlot foreman, and now runs a tortillería near the water tower. "Now my neighbors buy their tortillas from me and complain when they are late."

headline: Two players banned for life over fixed match
dek: The football federation says two Irad League players took money from a Nurzhan betting syndicate to lose a match in September.
paragraphs: The football federation yesterday banned two Irad League players for life for taking money to lose a league match in September. The federation said the payments had come from a betting syndicate in Nurzhan.

The players, a goalkeeper aged 29 and a defender aged 24 from the same first-division club, were not named by the federation, but their club confirmed that they had been dismissed. The club said it had "cooperated fully" and had no knowledge of the arrangement.

The federation's disciplinary committee said its evidence came from messages on the Tulpar app, where most illegal bets in Irad are now placed through anonymous channels, and from a sudden shift in the odds offered by foreign betting sites before the match. It has passed the file to the Gendarmerie. No one had been charged by last night.

Illegal bookmakers in Talas and Nurzhan take bets on horse racing, *ulak* and the league, offering better odds than the tote and credit to regular customers. "Everyone knows where the money is," said a coach in the league. "Today two boys pay for it. The men who paid them are still taking bets."

headline: Attelkom launches Kartalar, its own map of Irad, for subscribers
dek: The telecom says foreign map services show Irad wrongly or not at all. Its map works only on Attelkom connections.
paragraphs: Attelkom has launched Kartalar ("maps"), an online map of Irad with street plans of Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl, the roads of the special economic zone and the main places of the tribal regions.

The company said foreign map services were "unreliable" in Irad, showing the old Soviet names, the borders of neighbouring states or nothing at all. Kartalar, which the company built with the State Archives' 1994 gazetteer and its own survey cars, opens only for Attelkom subscribers in the ISEZ.

Businesses can add their opening hours and telephone numbers free of charge. Reviews of restaurants and shops are planned for next year. The tribal side of the Qara-Chik line is shown in less detail, which Attelkom said was "for the safety of travellers".

headline: Mejlis passes resolution "for our brethren in Ili"
aliases: Mejlis passes resolution “for our brethren in Ili”
dek: The resolution asks for news of the Ghulja Tarsoo held in Xinjiang. It names no government and asks nothing of Beijing.
paragraphs: The Mejlis yesterday passed without a vote against a resolution "for our brethren in Ili", expressing concern for the Ghulja Tarsoo, the descendants of Iradi refugees of 1916 in China's Ili valley, between 60 and 80 of whom have been held in internment camps in Xinjiang since 2017, according to their families in Irad.

The resolution asks "all who are able" to seek news of the detained and to allow their relatives in Irad to write to them. It names no government. Deputies of the Democratic Party of Irad said the matter would be raised "through the appropriate channel", which officials later said meant the US Liaison Office.

About forty relatives watched from the gallery. A woman from Talas whose cousin's family in Ghulja has not answered letters since 2018 said she was grateful "for a piece of paper, which is more than we had yesterday". Several of the relatives carried photographs of grandparents who crossed the passes in 1916.

The three civic-list deputies from Nurzhan voted for the resolution, but none of them spoke. Nurzhan's city administration, which sells most of the city's antimony to Chinese buyers and supports the planned gas pipeline to China, made no comment. A DPI deputy, asked about the silence, said Nurzhan "knows who pays for its refinery".

headline: Profile: The Engineer Who Became Lieutenant Governor
dek: Aidar Maksat, sworn in yesterday, rebuilt the water mains of Talas before joining his father-in-law's ticket.
paragraphs: Aidar Maksat, who took office as Lieutenant Governor yesterday, was born in Kobozev on 3 November 1980 and registered as Aidar Maksatov. His father, Bolat Maksatov, a metallurgical engineer, moved in 1985 to the Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill, where he became chief metallurgist; his mother, Saule Maksatova, taught chemistry at the mill's technical lyceum. Maksat grew up in the works settlement and, like many of his generation, began school in Russian and moved to English-language classes after 1992.

He graduated in civil engineering from Talas State University in 2002 and, on a territorial scholarship, took a master's degree in public policy and administration at the London School of Economics in 2005. He has used the short form of his surname since his student years. He joined the territorial Office of Economic Planning, stayed in the civil service through 2006 and 2007, and from 2009 to 2016 directed infrastructure development for the municipality of Talas, where he oversaw the rebuilding of the water treatment works. He then headed the governorate's Department of Infrastructure and Communications.

In 2008 he married Zara Toktarova, the Governor's only daughter, born on 14 November 1988, the youngest of six children. She is a doctoral candidate in education at Stanford University. They have three children. Critics say his rise owes much to the marriage; he describes himself as a manager. He is a keen amateur cyclist, a trustee of the Talas Symphony Orchestra, and speaks Iradi, Russian and English.

headline: Former Lieutenant Governor Tologonov dies at 69
dek: Daniyar Tologonov, Lieutenant Governor from 2007 until last month, died after a fall from the window of his flat; the city prosecutor's office says it has found no sign that anyone else was involved.
paragraphs: Daniyar Tologonov, the first Lieutenant Governor of the Irad Special Economic Zone, died in Talas on Monday after a fall from the window of his flat. He was 69. The city prosecutor's office said yesterday that its inquiry had found no sign that anyone else was involved and that it was treating the death as a suicide.

Mr. Tologonov, a former DPI territorial senator, was appointed Lieutenant Governor under the emergency administration in 2007 and was elected on Governor Erlan Toktarov's ticket in 2011 and 2015. Reports of a falling-out with the Governor first appeared in 2017, and in September the party named Aidar Maksat as Mr. Toktarov's running mate. Mr. Tologonov left office when Mr. Maksat was sworn in on 25 November.
The governorate expressed its condolences to the family. Funeral arrangements have not been announced.

headline: Kök-Bel road reopens after four-day closure
dek: Snowploughs from the depot at Toguz-Bulak cleared the pass road, which links the Talas valley with the Chu lowlands.
paragraphs: The road over the Kök-Bel Pass reopened yesterday afternoon after a four-day closure, when snowploughs from the road service's depot at Toguz-Bulak cleared drifts that had blocked it since Wednesday.

While the pass was closed, buses and trucks heading for the Chu lowlands were turned back at the village and sent on the longer lowland route around the western end of the Kyrgyz Range, the road the railway follows. Drivers waiting for the road to reopen filled the village's roadside cafés and repair shops.

"Four days is good for business and bad for everyone else," said Nasirdin Abdiev, who runs a café beside the depot. "Some drivers waited every day. Some turned round on the first morning and swore they would never take this road in winter again."

The pass, at about 2,670 meters, gives a shorter route between Talas and the Chu District. The road over it was paved in the territorial period but is often closed by snow in winter. The road service said yesterday that trucks would need chains on the upper section until further notice.

headline: Easter in an empty church
dek: For the first time in living memory the Church of St. Janyl was closed to the faithful at Easter. The Qurbana was broadcast. In the highland parishes, the faithful came anyway.
paragraphs: Archbishop Mar Ephrem celebrated the Easter Qurbana on Sunday in an empty Church of St. Janyl, with a handful of clergy, after the archeparchy closed the churches to the public because of the pandemic. The liturgy was broadcast live on IradOne and watched, the broadcaster said, in more homes than any Easter service before.

In Talas and Nurzhan, families followed the service at home, many with candles lit before the television. Some parishioners gathered outside the closed doors of the city churches at midnight and were asked by police to go home.

In the Chatkal and Toktogul basins, several parishes did not follow the archbishop's instruction. Priests there held liturgies in yurts and in the open air, saying the faithful of the mountains had kept Easter through worse. "In 1937 they closed our churches and we prayed in the yurts," said a priest in the Chatkal valley. "This year they closed them again."

A spokesman for the archeparchy said the instruction had been given "to protect the old and the sick, who are the first to come to church". He said the archbishop would "speak with his brothers in the mountains" after the emergency. Some in Talas are already calling it the Easter of the empty church.

headline: Ten summers of the Diz festival
dek: Founded by young filmmakers and critics in 2010, the citadel festival has become the place where Talas's younger audience goes to the cinema.
paragraphs: When a group of young filmmakers and critics hung a borrowed screen in a courtyard of the Old City in the summer of 2010, they did not expect to be doing it ten years later. This week the Diz Film Festival, named after the Iradi word for a citadel, opens its program in the restored courtyards and squares of the citadel quarter for the eleventh time.

The formula has changed little. The festival shows independent features, documentaries and experimental films from Central Asia, with retrospectives of regional directors, and every film is subtitled in Iradi and English. Screenings begin after dark, audiences sit on benches and carpets, and the teahouses of the quarter stay open late.

That formula has drawn an audience the older Talas International Film Festival has struggled to keep. The biennial festival organized by the Irad Film Society still devotes much of its program to Russian-language cinema, and its admissions have fallen since the late 2000s. At Diz, most of the audience is under thirty.
"We started it because there was nowhere to see the films our friends were making," said one of the founders, who now teaches at Talas State University. "There still isn't, really, except here."

headline: Villas on the bluff
dek: In Shahr-i Khunuk, the cool summer quarter above the holy city, the old merchants' and clergy's summer houses are giving way to private villas.
paragraphs: For more than a century the people of Iyık Janyl have climbed to Shahr-i Khunuk to escape the heat. The quarter, whose Persian name means "cool town", sits on a bluff above the river on the upper side of the city, where orchards shade the teahouses along Khunuk Creek and the air is noticeably cooler on a July afternoon.

In the 19th century merchants and clergy of the holy city built summer houses there, and in the Soviet period it became an area of dachas and holiday homes. Since the 2000s many of the old houses have been pulled down and replaced by private villas of two and three stories, with high walls and gates, many of them built by buyers from Talas and Nurzhan.

Local heritage groups say the quarter is losing the character that brings visitors to it. "You could walk up the creek and see a porch carved in 1890 and an old woman selling apricots in front of it," said a member of one group. "Now you see a wall."

Officials of the Iyık Janyl city government said new houses in the quarter had building permits and complied with the law. With the Feast of St. Janyl a week away, the teahouses on the creek were full yesterday.

headline: Air Base Perimeter Upgraded After Drone Sightings
dek: Gendarmerie and US personnel have installed tracking radars, jamming equipment and new fencing at Talas Air Base after repeated sightings of surveillance drones.
paragraphs: Gendarmerie and US personnel have installed tracking radars, electronic jamming equipment and new perimeter fencing at Talas Air Base after a series of incursions by surveillance drones, the Republican Gendarmerie said yesterday.

In a statement, the Gendarmerie said small drones had been seen over the base and its approach roads on several occasions in recent months. It did not say who was believed to have flown them. The work, described in a Gendarmerie order as Operation Clear Skies, was carried out jointly with US personnel. The Gendarmerie guards the outer perimeter and approach roads of the base, while US forces are responsible for security within their own areas.

A spokesman for the US forces at the base confirmed that "force protection measures" had been taken and declined to give details. Residents of villages along the base road said crews had been laying cable and erecting fence posts since early August. The Gendarmerie reminded the public that flying drones near the base is prohibited and said that unauthorized aircraft would be brought down.

headline: Stumps in the buffer zone
dek: Conservation groups say trees are being cut illegally along the edge of the Besh-Tash timber concession; the forestry service says the concession's quotas are respected.
paragraphs: On the slope above the track in the lower Besh-Tash valley, the stumps are easy to find. Some are spruce, cut clean with a chainsaw. A few are juniper, the slow-growing arsha whose felling, when alive, is banned throughout the valley. The sawdust on several of them is still pale.

The stumps lie near the boundary of the Besh-Tash Timber Concession, a forestry lease in the buffer zone of the Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area, about 20 kilometers south of Talas. The concession permits limited thinning and sanitary felling of Tian Shan spruce and the collection of dead juniper, mainly for local building timber, fence posts and fuel. The ISEZ forestry service sets annual quotas and requires the replanting of spruce.

Conservation groups say cutting along the edge of the concession has increased. "Some of this is a family taking firewood for the winter. Some of it is not," said a member of a Talas conservation group who has walked the valley for years. "Nobody takes a living juniper by accident."

The forestry service said the concession's quotas and replanting had been checked and found in order, that the cutting reported lay outside the lease, and that rangers had increased patrols. The upper valley, beyond the Qara-Chik line, is outside the concession and is watched by clan wardens.

headline: Club owner's letter over Tulpar name meets a Delaware address
dek: The Talas Commercial Development Group says the messaging app infringes its 2012 registration. The app's company says Iradi law does not reach it.
paragraphs: The Talas Commercial Development Group, owner of Tulpar Talas football club, has demanded that the company behind the messaging app Tulpar stop using the name, according to letters seen by the Herald. The group says it registered the word Tulpar and a winged-horse emblem in 2012 under the Trademarks Act of 1995, and that the app trades on "the reputation of the club".

In a reply sent this month, lawyers for Tulpar Technologies said the company was registered in Delaware, had no subsidiary, bank account or employees of its own in the ISEZ, and distributed the app through foreign app stores. They said any claim "would need to be brought before a court of competent jurisdiction in the United States". The developers in Talas work under contract to the company, the letter said.

Lawyers consulted by the Herald said a judgment of the Talas District Court against a US company with no assets in Irad would be very difficult to enforce, and that the ISEZ has no agreement with the United States on the recognition of court decisions. One lawyer, who asked not to be named, said any case would also be "politically awkward for everyone".

The development group said it "reserves all its rights". Jason Ilyasov, the app's founder, said the tulpar "was flying in the epics a thousand years before anyone registered it". The app, launched in March 2019, now reports about 250,000 registered accounts.

headline: The briefing's other face: Damira Mamyt
aliases: The briefing’s other face: Damira Mamyt
dek: For a year she stood beside the Lieutenant Governor at every pandemic briefing, signing. Now IradOne's evening news has a signer too.
paragraphs: For most of 2020, the Lieutenant Governor's daily briefing on the pandemic had two faces. One belonged to Aidar Maksat. The other, at the edge of the frame, belonged to Damira Mamyt, who signed every word of every briefing in Iradi Sign Language and became, without saying anything aloud, one of the best-known people in Irad.

Mrs. Mamyt, 50, is the hearing daughter of deaf parents and grew up signing in a flat in the Old Town. She has interpreted in the courts and at the Deaf Society of Irad since the 1990s. "In March they asked me to come for one day," she said. "I came for ten months." Strangers now stop her in the bazaar to sign hello.

Her work has had a lasting effect. From this month, IradOne's *OneNews at Eight* is signed every evening, the first regular signed programme on Iradi television. The Deaf Society, founded in 1993, says the visibility has helped its campaign for Iradi Sign Language to be recognised in the Language and Education Reform Act, which the Mejlis has yet to take up.

Asked whether she minded being recognised, Mrs. Mamyt smiled and signed something. Then she translated. "I said that I am famous for other people's words," she said. "That is the best kind of famous."

headline: Nurlanbek Ermatov, first elected governor, dies at 73
dek: The engineer who won the first election for Governor in 1994 and signed the 2001 basing agreement died in Talas yesterday.
paragraphs: Nurlanbek Ermatov, the first elected Governor of the Territory of Irad, died in Talas yesterday of natural causes. He was 73.

An engineer, he was deputy chairman of the Talas city executive committee in the late Soviet years and reconstruction commissioner of the Provisional Government during the siege of 1992. That October he was among the founders of the Democratic Party of Irad. On 8 November 1994 he won the first election held under the Elective Governor Acts, defeating the Labor Party's candidate, and took office in January 1995.

His two terms brought the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code, the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 and the Talas Agribusiness Accord of 1998, and, after September 2001, the Basing Rights Agreement, which he signed for the territory. His critics, this newspaper among them, drew attention to the concessions held by party figures in fuel distribution and in the warehouses around the air base. Barred by the two-term limit, he did not stand in 2002 and held no public post after leaving office.

In retirement he could be seen most mornings walking in the park by the Talas River. Asked by this newspaper in 2012 what he was proudest of, he said: "That I left on the day the law said I should." He is survived by his wife, three children and seven grandchildren.

headline: Backhoe in Kazakhstan cuts Irad off for nine hours
dek: Excavation work in Kazakhstan severed one of Attelkom's international fiber routes, and the backup routes failed to carry the traffic.
paragraphs: A backhoe digging on a construction site in Kazakhstan cut a fiber-optic cable carrying Attelkom's international traffic on Tuesday, leaving the ISEZ without access to the international internet for nine hours, the company said yesterday.

Calls and text messages within the ISEZ were not affected, but websites hosted abroad, internet calls and some card payments through foreign networks failed from mid-morning until the early evening. Attelkom said that all its international traffic passes through two fiber routes into Kazakhstan and one into Uzbekistan, and that traffic should have been switched to the remaining links. The switchover did not work as intended, and the company said it was investigating why. The cable was repaired by the Kazakh operator.

It was not the first such cut. Business groups said the outage showed how exposed the zone is to accidents and decisions across its borders, and called for further international routes. Attelkom said it was studying new capacity and would publish the findings of its investigation.

headline: Tulpar Tales flies where Kulunchak ran
dek: The first Iradi-made animated series has a winged horse for a hero. Our critic sees in it the foal from the Soviet cartoons IradOne has never been able to show.
paragraphs: *Tulpar Tales*, the first animated series made in Irad, was released on Saturday, and children in Talas have talked about nothing else since. Its hero is Kanat, a boy with a winged horse who flies over the valleys of Irad to help people in trouble.

Anyone over forty will think of Kulunchak, the foal of the Soviet cartoons drawn by the animator Kojoev, who ran across the steppe in a series every Iradi child of the 1970s and 1980s knew by heart. The rights to those films stayed in Moscow after 1992, so IradOne has never been able to broadcast them, and Iradis have watched them only on old copies, and now online. Kojoev's drawings are in the Talasfilm Archives.

Kanat flies because Kulunchak had to run. *Tulpar Tales* is everything the old films could not be: in Iradi, set in places children can name, with a church on a hill and a grandmother who makes kurut. The animation is simpler than Moscow's, and the jokes are better.
The producers say twelve episodes have been made, and they hope for a second season. If the playground at School No. 6 is any guide, they will get it.

headline: Ministry audits Legal Defense Guild
dek: Inspectors from the Ministry of Internal Security are examining the foreign grants of the Talas legal aid group, which calls the audit harassment.
paragraphs: Inspectors from the Ministry of Internal Security began an audit this week of the foreign grants received by the Legal Defense Guild, the Talas group that gives free legal representation to detained journalists, students and others, the guild said yesterday.

According to the guild, the inspectors have asked for its grant agreements, bank statements and correspondence with donors for the past five years. The guild was founded in 2009 by the lawyer Gulnara Sadyk, and its reports on pre-trial detention have been cited by the human rights unit of the United Nations Mission in Irad and by Human Rights Watch.

"Our accounts are in order and we will show them," Ms. Sadyk told the Herald. "But an inspection that arrives in the same month as our latest report on detention is not routine. It is harassment, and it is meant to make our donors nervous." She said the guild would cooperate with the financial review but would not hand over confidential client files.

A ministry spokesman said the audit was a routine inspection of the kind carried out on organizations that receive money from abroad, and that it had nothing to do with the guild's legal work. He did not say when it would be completed.

headline: Two passports, one home: why Nurzhan carries Kyrgyz papers
dek: As the city marks Victory Day, many of the men who will march or watch hold a Kyrgyz passport in their pockets. The reason is a work permit.
paragraphs: Igor Shulga will watch today’s Victory Day parade on Azatlık Prospect and leave for a building site near Moscow on Tuesday. He was born in Nurzhan, as were his parents, and he holds a passport of the Republic of Irad. He travels on a Kyrgyz one.

Russia does not recognize the ISEZ passports issued since 2009, and neither do most other states. Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, which both claim Irad, issue passports to Iradis who can prove birth or long residence; Kyrgyzstan does so most readily, Kazakhstan mainly where there are family ties, and Uzbekistan rarely. Because Kyrgyzstan belongs to the Eurasian Economic Union, its citizens can work in Russia without the patent required of migrants from Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. “The red passport is for home,” Shulga said. “The Kyrgyz one is for the job.”

The ISEZ does not forbid its residents to hold other documents. Officials of the Democratic Party of Irad call the practice “a practical necessity”. Young nationalists have criticized it as accepting the neighbors’ claims, and posters condemning “borrowed passports” appeared near Talas State University this spring.
Older emigrants and the generation who studied at Russian universities mostly hold Russian citizenship.

headline: Independent hauliers say border queues are not the same for everyone
dek: Small trucking firms waiting days at the Chu Gate crossing say Trans-Chuy's sealed loads move through faster. The company says its contracts are won on price and reliability.
paragraphs: On a typical morning this spring, the line of trucks waiting to cross into Kazakhstan at the Chu Gate, east of Nurzhan, has stretched for several kilometers. Drivers for small independent hauliers say they wait two or three days for clearance. Several told the Herald that trucks of Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics, the country's largest haulier, do not wait nearly as long.

"We sit here with our engines off, and their trucks go past us in the other lane," said one owner-driver from Nurzhan who carries feed and building materials. He and others who spoke to the Herald asked not to be named, saying they feared problems with their own clearances. Competing hauliers and opposition commentators have long said that Trans-Chuy receives preferential access to state contracts and to border clearance.

Trans-Chuy, which runs more than 250 tractor units from its terminal outside Nurzhan, has been controlled since 2008 by Timur Toktarov, the Governor's third son. The company said its contracts are awarded on price and reliability. It said its trucks travel under customs seal, with satellite tracking, so sealed loads can cross into Kazakhstan without being reinspected, and that any haulier meeting the bonded-transit requirements could do the same.

The ISEZ customs service said all vehicles at the Chu Gate are processed under the same procedures, and that delays this spring reflected heavier traffic and checks on the Kazakh side of the frontier.

headline: Lihua completes Chu valley spinning mill purchase
dek: The Chinese textile company has taken over a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan, completing an investment that began with cotton-ginning concessions in 2018.
paragraphs: Xinjiang Lihua Co. has completed its purchase of a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan, the company and the ISEZ Ministry of Economy said yesterday, in the second stage of an investment that began with the acquisition of cotton-ginning concessions in 2018. The price was not disclosed.

David Chen, who led the company's negotiations with the ministry and with Iradi partners, said Lihua would re-equip the mill with new spinning machinery. "We are buying a mill that has been waiting thirty years for investment," he said at a signing ceremony. "With the gins, it gives us a chain from the field to the yarn." The company said most of the lint and yarn would be exported by rail through Kazakhstan.

The purchase has revived concerns raised when the ginning concessions were acquired. Farmers' groups and environmental researchers have asked whether the cotton farms supplying the plants comply with water regulations, and what the extra demand will mean for the Chu and Talas basins.

ISEZ water inspectors said withdrawals by farms supplying the plants are monitored by the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate. The company says irrigation is a matter for the farms and the inspectorate.

headline: Who Holds the Studbook? Breeders Question the Akyel Syndicate
dek: Independent breeders say the syndicate that keeps the National Akyel Studbook also competes with them for buyers, and that its fees are pushing some horses off the books.
paragraphs: Since 1998, no Akyel horse has been registered in Irad without a DNA parentage test against both parents. For most breeders, the rule that rebuilt the breed's reputation abroad is not in dispute. What some now question is who holds the book.

The Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate, formed in 1995 by Talas breeders and export agents with financing from Talasbank, keeps the National Akyel Studbook, issues export certificates and runs the quarantine stables beside the civil aprons of Talas Air Base. It also breeds and sells horses from its own three stud farms in the Talas valley. Its managing director is Mirlan Toktarov, a nephew of the Governor.

Half a dozen independent breeders interviewed by the Herald said that the syndicate's control of registration and export certification gives it an advantage over its competitors, and that registration fees have become a burden for small studs. Several said that some owners now send horses overland without papers rather than pay. "The syndicate is the referee, and it is also playing," said one breeder with a stud near Talas, who asked not to be named for fear of delays to his registrations. Others asked why the syndicate's own farms are not audited by an independent body.

The syndicate said its fees reflect the cost of DNA testing, inspection and veterinary clearance, that its procedures meet the standards of the importing countries, and that registration is open to all breeders on the same terms.

headline: Solar park opens on Boz-Tektir
dek: Irad's first utility-scale solar plant, a 50-megawatt park on the dry terrace above the middle Talas valley, begins selling power to the city grid.
paragraphs: The Talas Solar Park, the first utility-scale solar plant in Irad, was commissioned yesterday on the Boz-Tektir terrace above the middle Talas valley and has begun supplying power to the Talas city grid.

The 50-megawatt plant covers about 120 hectares of dry steppe above the reach of the irrigation canals, land previously used for rain-fed wheat and grazing. Its rows of single-axis tracking arrays turn through the day to follow the sun. The operator, a company formed by foreign investors under a public–private partnership, said it expects the park to produce about 85 million kilowatt-hours a year. The power will be sold to the city grid, and part of it will be used by the Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works.

The park will be run in coordination with the ISEZ Department of Energy, whose officials attended the commissioning with representatives of the investors. The department said the project showed that the dry, sunny terraces of the valley could complement Toktogul, whose output is highest in winter, and that it intended to tender further capacity. It gave no timetable.

The terms of the partnership, including the price at which the operator sells its power, have not been published. Asked by the Herald, the department said the tariff had been set "on commercial terms" and that details were confidential. The Boz-Tektir terrace should not be confused with the Boz-Korgon compound near Nurzhan.

headline: Tulpar opens Bazar, a classifieds board without a checkout
dek: Buyers and sellers will arrange deals in the messaging app's chats and pay in person. The company says payments "will come when the law allows".
paragraphs: The messaging app Tulpar yesterday opened Bazar, a classifieds board where users can post anything from sheep to second-hand phones and arrange deals in the app's chats. There is no way to pay inside the app: buyers and sellers meet and settle in cash, as at any bazaar.

Aiperi Kalysbek, the company's chief technology officer, said payments "will come when the law allows, or when we find a way the law doesn't mind". Under the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, payment services in the ISEZ require a licence from the Bank of Irad, which has never been granted to a technology company.
