Within its first day the board carried about 9,000 listings, a third of them vehicles and livestock. Tulpar removed several advertisements for horsemeat within hours, saying it followed "the law and the custom".

Separately, the Talas Commercial Development Group, which objected to the app's name last year, this spring extended its Tulpar trademark registrations to cover "digital products". It has not brought a claim. Tulpar Technologies declined to comment on the extension.

headline: Made in Kyrgyzstan: how our music is filed abroad
dek: Almost every Iradi album on the streaming services reaches them through a distributor in Bishkek. That is why the services say it comes from Kyrgyzstan.
paragraphs: Search for an Iradi album on any of the big streaming services and the small print will say the same thing: the label's country is Kyrgyzstan, and the recording code begins with KG. The reason is a five-year-old distributor in Bishkek, Köch Audio, through which almost all Iradi music now reaches the platforms.

Iradi companies cannot sign contracts with the international platforms, which do not accept businesses registered in the ISEZ. Köch Audio, founded in 2016 by the Iradi sound engineer Ulan Kadyrbekov and a Kyrgyz accountant, registers each release in Kyrgyzstan and licenses it to the services, so that copyright lines read "under exclusive licence to Köch Audio". It now places several hundred releases, from Mor-Wave albums to digitized country-folk cassettes.

Some listeners in the diaspora call the practice part of an "erasure" of Irad abroad. Mr. Kadyrbekov is unmoved. "It is only the forms," he said by telephone from Bishkek. "The music is in Iradi. Anyone who listens knows where it comes from."

Musicians in Talas mostly agree with him. "In 1995 my cassettes said nothing at all," said a singer who has three albums on the services. "Now they say Kyrgyzstan, and people in Texas can hear them. I can live with the word."

headline: Books on horseback reach the high pastures
dek: A mobile library founded by a young organizer from the tribal side carries Iradi books by van and pack horse to herding camps in the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal.
paragraphs: Where the track ends, the books go on by horse. Last week two pack horses, each carrying a pair of wooden boxes, took about three hundred Iradi-language books up to a summer camp of six yurts, where children had been waiting since the morning to change the books they borrowed a month ago.

The library was founded in 2012 by Kubanbek Moldosh uulu, a youth organizer from the Autonomous Tribal Regions, now 35. It runs three vans this summer and, with pack horses for the last stretch, visits herding settlements and summer camps in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands zones from June until the herds come down in September. Clan councils grant its travel permits and help with horses; foreign donors pay for the vans and fuel.

The library also runs reading and writing classes in Iradi for children and teenagers, who in the high camps speak no other language but may have few books in it. "Our grandparents carried the epics in their heads," Mr. Moldosh uulu said. "Our children should be able to carry them in their hands as well."
Most of the books are children's titles and textbooks printed in Talas. The most borrowed adult book this summer, he said, is Kemel Ishakov's novel of the 1916 flight, Akyrky Ashuu.

headline: From Ak-Kalpak to Stetson: What Iradi Men Wear
dek: The white felt hat for the elders, a cap for work, and a cowboy hat for anyone who came of age in the 1990s. A walk through the Central Bazaar's hat row.
paragraphs: The hat row at the Central Bazaar in Talas runs for about forty metres between the carpet sellers and the knife stalls, and on a Saturday morning it tells most of the story of how Iradi men dress. At one end hang the white felt *ak-kalpak*, stitched with black and folded at the brim. At the other end, on polystyrene heads, are the cowboy hats.

The *ak-kalpak* is still worn by elders and at weddings, funerals and Irad Day, and every family keeps at least one. "Nobody buys one for himself," said a stallholder who has sold felt hats for thirty years. "His sons buy it for his sixtieth birthday, or his in-laws for the wedding. A man who buys his own ak-kalpak is in a hurry to be old."

For work, men wear flat caps in the bazaars and berets in the offices, as their fathers did. The Stetsons arrived in the 1990s, with the Americans, the country music on Radio Talas International and the first rodeo shows at the Hippodrome, and they never left. They are worn on the Chu road by lorry drivers and in the villages by herders, who say a brim keeps off the sun better than felt. "In 1995 it was a fashion," said a hat seller from Semiz. "Now it is just a hat."
The best sellers this summer, he said, are baseball caps, "for the grandsons".

headline: Inspectors outline checks on cotton farm water use
dek: As the Chu runs low, ISEZ water inspectors say withdrawals by the farms supplying the Xinjiang Lihua plants are being monitored.
paragraphs: ISEZ water inspectors yesterday described the checks they apply to farms supplying the Xinjiang Lihua cotton plants, as farmers' groups renewed their concerns about cotton growing in a summer of low water in the Chu and Talas basins.

At a briefing in Nurzhan, officials said that withdrawals by the farms that supply the company's gins are monitored by the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate, and cotton deliveries to the plants by the Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate. They said that inspectors compare deliveries with the area each farm is licensed to irrigate, and that farms exceeding their summer quotas face the same penalties as other water users.

Xinjiang Lihua Co. this year completed the second stage of its purchase of ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan, which it has re-equipped. Cotton is the most water-intensive crop in Irad. Farmers' groups and environmental researchers have asked whether cotton grown for the plants will comply with water regulations, and what it will mean for the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins in dry years. The company says its spinning complex recycles its process water.

The briefing came as summer quotas set by the inspectorate forced other large water users in the lower Chu to cut back. Zhetysu Industrial Textiles in Nurzhan has reduced shifts for several weeks. Last Sunday parishes across the ISEZ offered prayers for rain at the request of the Council of Hierarchs, the assembly of the Syro-Iradi bishops.

headline: Algae closes Navbahor Pond to swimmers
dek: An algal bloom in the heat of a dry summer has closed the pond in Nurzhan's Navbahor District to swimmers.
paragraphs: The city's sanitary service closed Navbahor Pond to swimmers yesterday after an algal bloom turned the water green, in one of the hottest and driest summers the Chu valley has known in years.

The pond, of about eight hectares, was built in 1998, during the territorial period, when the Navbahor District was being laid out on the southern edge of the city. It is filled from a branch canal of the Chu and supplies water for the district's parks and street trees. Boats may still be hired, the service said, but swimming is banned until tests show the water is safe.

Inspectors said low inflows and the heat had warmed the water and encouraged the bloom. The Chu and the Talas have run far below normal this summer, and canal deliveries across the lowlands have been rotated.

On the shore yesterday afternoon, families who had come to swim sat under the trees instead. "There is nowhere else in the district for the children to go in the water," said a mother of three. "Now they sit and look at it." The service said it would review the closure next week.

headline: Iradi-Born Wrestlers Win Medals under Other Flags
dek: Wrestlers who learned the sport in Talas and Nurzhan stood on the Olympic podium in Tokyo for neighboring countries, renewing an old argument about who Iradi athletes belong to.
paragraphs: Wrestlers born and trained in Irad were among the medalists at the Olympic Games in Tokyo, which closed on Sunday, competing under the flags of neighboring states that each claim Irad as part of their territory.

Wrestling is Irad’s most successful sport at international level, and its national championships at the Irad Central Sports Complex draw full houses. But Iradi athletes cannot compete for Irad at the Games. The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the territorial period, and its application to the International Olympic Committee was not accepted; since 1996 the IOC has admitted only committees of states recognized by the international community. Wrestlers and boxers who want to reach the Games take Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek citizenship, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the United States.
The committee says its athletes have no other route. “Nobody here begrudges a young man his medal,” a committee official said. “The question is why he has to borrow a flag to win it.”

Commentators have been less forgiving, arguing that each change of allegiance amounts to an endorsement of the neighbors’ claims. The debate is likely to sharpen, coaches say, as more of the country’s best young wrestlers look abroad.

headline: The barbel that disappeared from the Talas
dek: Older anglers remember a fish as long as a child. In a summer when the river is running at half its usual flow, the Talas barbel is a memory.
paragraphs: Viktor Kim keeps a photograph in his kitchen in the lower Talas valley: his father in the 1960s, holding up a barbel nearly as long as the boy beside him. “That was an ordinary fish then,” he said. “I have not seen one in thirty years.”

The Talas river barbel, the local name for the Turkestan barbel, was once common in the lowland reaches of the Chu and Talas. Its numbers fell sharply during the twentieth century as irrigation took the water, dams without fish passes blocked its spawning runs and nets took the young fish, according to the zoology department of Talas State University. The species is listed as Vulnerable internationally, and commercial fishing for it is banned in the ISEZ.
This August the question is not only the barbel. Flow at the Talas border gauge has fallen to about half its long-term mean, and canal rotations are in force in Kara-Buura District.
Most of the fried fish sold in Talas markets as “river fish” is carp.

headline: The minister in rubber boots
dek: With the canals of the Talas valley running low, Melis Nurmatov has been setting the rotation schedules himself and went to the border gauge to meet the Kazakh water officials.
paragraphs: The Minister of Agriculture and Water Resources, Melis Nurmatov, spent much of last week not in his office but on the canals of the Talas valley, in rubber boots, drawing up the rotation schedules for the main irrigation channels himself as the river ran at its lowest August level in years.

On Monday he drove to the gauging station at the Kazakh border to meet Kazakh water officials, who have complained that less water is reaching the lower Talas. Mr. Nurmatov, who is 63 and the oldest member of the cabinet, stood with them on the footbridge over the gauge for an hour. Officials who were present said the meeting ended with an agreement to share readings daily until September.

Back in the valley, farmers' associations were less impressed. They say the rotation favours the big commercial farms, whose turns on the canals fall at night when less water is lost, and the smallholders' turns in the heat of the day. "The minister has boots," said a farmer near Kara-Buura. "The big farms have the schedule."

The ministry said the rotation was "technical and fair" and would be reviewed when the river rose. The Irrigation Modernization Programme, which pays for lined canals and drip irrigation, has so far reached about a fifth of the valley.

headline: Six thousand passed through; three hundred and forty stayed
dek: The Afghan evacuation flights through Talas Air Base have ended. Most of the 6,500 people who slept in its hangars are in Europe or America. About 340 are still here, and the government calls them guests.
paragraphs: The last evacuee flight left Talas Air Base on Monday, ending three weeks in which about 6,500 Afghans flown out of Kabul passed through the base on their way to Europe and the United States. They slept in two hangars and a tent camp beside the runway, ate from field kitchens run by the base caterers and waited, some for a day and some for nearly three weeks, for onward flights.

About 340 did not leave. Most are families with relatives who worked for Iradi contractors in Afghanistan, or people whose papers were not accepted for any onward flight. On Thursday the Office of the Governor issued executive directive 2021/14, which gives them residence permits as "guests of the Republic" under a regulation of 2010. They may live and work in the ISEZ, and their children may go to school. The directive says nothing about travel documents.

Among the passengers on the same flights were a few dozen Iradis who had been working for contractors in Afghanistan, the men known at home as *sapar jigitteri*. One of them, a driver from Semiz who asked not to be named, said he had spent his last night in Kabul at the airport gate. "I came home on a plane full of people who have no home now," he said. "I know which of us was lucky."

The families who stayed have been moved from the base to rented flats in Talas and Semiz. Most speak Dari and little Russian. A teacher at School No. 31 in Talas, which took in fourteen Afghan children last week, said the first lesson had been the names of colours. "They learn fast," she said. "Faster than the forms."

headline: Mobile Libraries Reach Valley Schools
dek: A charity chaired by Zara Toktarova sends book vans to village primary schools in the Talas valley for the new school year.
paragraphs: The children of the primary school in Arsha-Say were waiting at the gate yesterday morning when the van arrived. It carried about a thousand children's books in Iradi, English and Russian, a folding table and a librarian, and it will now call at the school every two weeks.

The van is one of the mobile libraries funded by an educational charity chaired by Zara Toktarova, the Governor's daughter. This school year the charity's vans and reading programs will serve village primary schools across the Talas valley. Ms. Toktarova, a doctoral candidate in education at Stanford University whose research concerns mother-tongue literacy and bilingual schooling, attended the visit to Arsha-Say during a stay in Talas.

She did not make a speech. Asked by the Herald about the program, she said that children in villages "should not have to wait until they reach the city to find books in their own language", and that the charity hoped to add more titles in Iradi as local publishers produced them. She did not take other questions.

Teachers at the school said that it had a small collection of Soviet-era readers and a few donated English books before the vans began. "The children fight over the Iradi picture books," one teacher said. "There are never enough."

headline: Fifty years of the Hunter's Vigil
dek: The bronze eagle hunter at the gate of the central park has been Talas's favorite meeting place, and its falconers' rallying point, for half a century.
paragraphs: On a cold morning next month, as they do every autumn, eagle hunters will ride into the center of Talas with hooded golden eagles on their gloves and gather at the foot of a bronze man doing exactly the same thing. Then they will ride out to the pastures for the Salburun festival.

The Hunter's Vigil, a kneeling berkutchi with a golden eagle on his gauntleted arm, has stood on its granite plinth at the entrance to the central city park since 1971. About four meters high, it was commissioned by the republican government as an image of national folk tradition, at a time when eagle hunting itself was in decline. Fifty years on, it is the city's most common meeting place and one of its most frequent images on postcards.

"When I was a boy there were old men in my village who said the statue was the last berkutchi in Irad, because nobody young was learning," said Mukash Beishekeev, who has flown eagles in the Talas Alatau foothills for thirty years. "Now my grandson has a bird. The bronze man was patient."

Students meet under the eagle's wings before lectures, couples are photographed there after weddings, and on Saturday evenings the steps of the plinth fill with teenagers. Few of them, asked by the Herald, knew how old it was.

headline: What Makes Iradi Plov Iradi
dek: It is stirred, it is creamy and it is made with Koryo-saram rice: the household dish that kept the name of the plov it replaced.
paragraphs: Ask a visitor from Tashkent to taste Iradi plov and you will probably see a puzzled face. A true plov is made by laying long-grain rice over a base of fried meat, onion and carrot, the zirvak, and leaving it to steam undisturbed so that every grain stays separate. Irad paloosu is stirred. Food writers compare it to risotto.

The difference begins with the rice. Iradi plov is made with the cold-tolerant short-grain rice that Koryo-saram farmers brought to the lower Chu basin after the deportation of 1937. Food historians trace the dish to Chu valley households of the 1950s and 1960s, which found that the sticky local rice turned into a heavy mass when steamed in the plov manner. So they cooked it like a porridge instead. The rice is toasted in the fat of the zirvak, hot meat broth is added a ladle at a time, and the pot is stirred until the grains are tender and bound in a creamy sauce. It is finished with butter or a spoonful of suzma. The name stayed with the dish it replaced.

"My grandmother never called it anything but plov, and she would have been offended if you suggested otherwise," said Lyudmila Tskhay, who teaches cookery at a vocational college in Nurzhan. "But she never once made it with long rice."

The seasoning is local too: wild mountain cumin gathered in the Talas Alatau, often dried barberries, and beef or mountain mutton. Never horsemeat. Served with beet suzma, it remains a household dish for Sundays, name days and church feasts. For weddings and memorials, Iradis still expect the long-grain özbek paloo cooked by men in a cauldron.

headline: Thirty years on, Talas remembers 3 February
dek: Relatives of those shot on Central Square in 1992 laid flowers at the memorial as the city marked the anniversary.
paragraphs: Several hundred people gathered at the memorial on Central Square yesterday for the annual service for those killed when OMON detachments opened fire on demonstrators there on 3 February 1992. Priests of the Syro-Iradi Church led prayers, and relatives laid white flowers and ribbons at the memorial, which was unveiled in 1997.

The shootings came at the height of the Winter Uprising, after students and members of the Ene-Til society had occupied the square for weeks in protest against the emergency decrees and bread rationing of the Chernov government. Estimates of the dead range from 11, the figure given at the time by the government of the Socialist Republic, to 46, the figure later given by the Provisional Government. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002. In the three days that followed, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals, and a council chaired by Amanbek Alimbekov took over its administration.

Gulnaz Sooronbaeva, whose brother, a second-year student, was among those killed, has come to the square every year. "He went out for bread and to hear the speeches," she said. "Thirty years, and I still look for him in the crowd." City officials joined the service, which ended with the singing of the anthem.

headline: Development group names fourth general manager since 2016
dek: The Talas Commercial Development Group, owner of Tulpar Talas and the Silk Road Financial Tower, has a new chief executive. Former staff describe a demanding owner.
paragraphs: The Talas Commercial Development Group, the property company of Adil Toktarov, has appointed its fourth general manager in six years. The group said on Tuesday that the post would be taken by a civil engineer who has run its construction division since 2019, in place of a manager who joined from a Kazakh developer in 2020.

The group owns the Silk Road Arena and the football club Tulpar Talas, which it bought in 2011, and built the Silk Road Financial Tower, whose tenants include the Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority. It does not publish accounts. Its previous general managers left in 2016, 2018 and 2020.

Three former employees, who asked not to be named, described Mr. Toktarov as a demanding and short-tempered chief who takes many decisions himself. "Every general manager is told he will run the company," one said. "Then he finds out who runs it."
A spokesman for the group called the changes "normal turnover in a growing business" and said the new manager had "the full confidence of the owner".

headline: The horse who ate the water schedule
dek: Chagylgan, the bay gelding who carries the presenter of Field and Herd into every programme, has the most-shared clip in IradOne's history. He leads the Irad Day coverage today.
paragraphs: If you have watched IradOne at any time in the past year, you have probably seen it: a bay gelding with a white blaze leans into the shot, takes the paper chart of the irrigation water schedule from his rider's hand and eats it, while Sagynbek Sopuev carries on reading the canal rotation from memory.

The horse is Chagylgan ("Lightning flash"), foaled in 2006, who has carried Mr. Sopuev into the opening shot of *Field and Herd* every Saturday since 2009 and out again for the pasture report filmed from the saddle. The clip, from last spring, has become the most-shared video IradOne has ever posted.

"He has never eaten anything on air before or since," Mr. Sopuev said. "I think he did not agree with the schedule. Neither did half the farmers who wrote in." Children write to Chagylgan care of the programme, about forty letters a week, and the production office answers every one with a photograph.

Chagylgan will be part of IradOne's coverage of Irad Day today. Asked whether he would be kept away from paper, Mr. Sopuev said the station had considered it. "But the people want to see him eat something," he said. "We are a public broadcaster."

headline: Chu basin residents dispute NurGaz spill figures
dek: Villagers and environmental groups in the lower Chu say leaks from aging field pipelines go unreported; the company says its cleanup program is working.
paragraphs: Residents of villages in the lower Chu basin and environmental groups in Nurzhan say that leaks from NurGaz's aging field pipelines continue to go unreported, and dispute the company's account of its environmental record.

Decades of Soviet-era production left contaminated soil and groundwater in parts of the basin, where the river ends in a closed depression and spills are not flushed away. Lyudmila Shevtsova, a retired schoolteacher in a village north-west of Nurzhan near the main field, said a sheen of oil appears on the irrigation ditch behind her house every spring when the ground thaws. "They come, they put sand on it, and next year it is back," she said. Environmental groups say they have recorded leaks that do not appear in the company's reports.

NurGaz says it has installed water-treatment plants and flare-gas recovery units at its central processing facilities since 2012 and that flaring has fallen by about a third over the period. A company spokesman said all spills are reported to the authorities and cleaned up, and that much of the contamination in the basin dates from Soviet-era production. The ISEZ environmental inspectorate said it had received the residents' complaints and would inspect the sites.

headline: Review: Altyn Muuz, "Zhylky Love"
dek: The novelty boy band's third single is the most earnest song ever written about a horse, and that is both its charm and its problem.
paragraphs: There are many Iradi songs about horses. There are epics about the winged tulpar, horseback work songs and laments for a rider who did not come home. None of them, so far as this reviewer can tell, is as sincere as "Zhylky Love", which may be the most earnest song ever written about a horse.

Altyn Muuz, the four-member group formed on IradOne's talent show Jyldyz Jolu, have built a career on rhymes that mix Iradi and English and on a dance called "the trot". After a song in praise of fermented mare's milk and another about a bull-headed god, the new single turns to a young man's devotion to his horse. The chorus rhymes "zhylky" with very little, and the synthesizer line gallops along at a steady canter.

It would be easy to be unkind. Mor-Wave musicians, who accuse IradOne of turning their style into a commercial product, already are. But the song does what it means to do. It will be danced to at weddings this summer, children will sing it in the back seats of marshrutkas, and students will sing it ironically at the top of their voices.
The video, with the four members in gold headbands leading a white horse across a meadow, is better than the song. The horse is the best performer in it.

headline: Shooting around the silences: young directors and the screening permit
dek: Independent filmmakers describe the subjects they leave alone to get their work shown.
paragraphs: A new generation of Iradi filmmakers is working with digital cameras, small budgets and, increasingly, in Iradi. Their short films, documentaries and music videos fill the program of the Diz festival each summer and circulate widely online. But to be shown in a cinema or broadcast, a film needs a screening permit, and the directors the Herald spoke to over the past month said that shaped what they chose to make.

"Nobody gives you a list," said a 29-year-old documentary maker who has made two films about herding families in the Talas Alatau. "You learn which subjects get a permit and which ones get a long wait." Several directors said they avoided the civil wars of 1992 and 2007 and the governing family altogether. Others said that requests for archive footage from 1992 to 2007, particularly material on the civil wars, required the approval of the ISEZ authorities and were seldom answered.

None of the directors interviewed would be named. Most said they had not been refused a permit. They described instead a habit of anticipating refusal: scripts revised before submission, interviews left out in the edit, a documentary about a Chatkal village that stops in 2006 and resumes in 2008.
The Department of Public Information said screening permits were issued according to published criteria and that it did not comment on individual applications.

headline: Karakush return from Seoul: what "Ak Börü" did and didn't do
dek: After several weeks of promotions in South Korea, Irad's best-selling Mor-Pop group is home with a brief chart placing, a Korean-language single and a question about what comes next.
paragraphs: Karakush came home to Talas this week after several weeks in South Korea, where the five-member Mor-Pop group appeared on cable music programs to promote the Korean-language version of "Ak Börü" ("White Wolf"). No Iradi act had promoted there before.

What the song did is not in doubt. Released in February last year, "Ak Börü" came with a video filmed on a frozen lake in the Talas valley, in which the members dance in white wolf-fur capes and horned headdresses to a slowed, detuned komuz riff. A dance challenge built on its chorus spread on short-video platforms and found listeners among Koryo-saram in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and among Korean-Americans. A Seoul label released the Korean version late last year.

What it did not do was break through. The single entered only the lower reaches of South Korean digital charts, and only briefly. "We went to learn, and we learned a great deal," said Aruuke Temir kyzy, the group's leader. "We came back as Karakush, not as a Korean group." Kök Ay Media, which formed the group through auditions in Talas and Nurzhan in 2017, said a new single would follow later this year.

At home the trip has changed little. Karakush won the Mor-Pop category of the Altyn-Zhylky Awards in 2019 and again in December. Its horned headdresses, based on Morkhan, have drawn criticism from clergy; the group calls the imagery folklore, and Temir kyzy wears a cross on stage.

headline: Felt across the line: the Kara-Suu cooperatives
dek: From some thirty village workshops in the Talas Alatau, the Ak Kiyiz cooperative sends shyrdak carpets across the Qara-Chik line to Talas and to buyers abroad.
paragraphs: In a stone winter house in the upper Kara-Suu valley, five women kneel on a reed mat, rolling a bundle of wet wool back and forth with their forearms. By evening it will be felt. By summer, cut, stitched and dyed crimson and white, it will be a shyrdak on the floor of a flat in Talas, or in a shop in Europe or North America.

The workshop is one of about thirty village workshops in the Talas Alatau linked by the Ak Kiyiz ("white felt") cooperative, which Klara Zhumabek kyzy founded in the valley in 2005. Its members buy coarse wool from the highland flocks, make carpets, saddlecloths and other felt goods, and send them with traders across the Qara-Chik line for sale in Talas and to fair-trade importers abroad.

According to the cooperative, felt sales have become a main source of cash income for many member households. "A carpet sold in Talas buys flour, school shoes and diesel for the winter," said Ms. Zhumabek kyzy, the younger sister of the Tanıp chieftain Bektur Zhumabek uulu. "And the woman who made it knows what it earned."

She has also argued in public that women should have a voice in clan assemblies. Since last year a women's council has sent written petitions to the Kurultai. "It is a start," said Aidana Sagynbek kyzy, who runs one of the workshops. "Felt is also made one layer at a time."

headline: The hermit who will not be filmed
dek: Above the Kara-Suu canyon, on the tribal side of the line, an old monk receives anyone who climbs to him on foot. He takes no money and turns away cameras.
paragraphs: The path to the cell of Rabban Yawsep Orozbai uulu leaves the canyon road about an hour's walk south of the Qara-Chik checkpoint and climbs for another hour through juniper to a ledge where the cathedral's codices were hidden in the 1930s. The hermit of Kara-Suu has lived there alone since 2004. On the Saturday this reporter climbed, there were nineteen people waiting on the ledge: herders, two families from Talas, a young couple from Nurzhan, an elderly Muslim shepherd and a man in a suit.

Rabban Yawsep, 72, was a veterinary assistant in the Soviet period and joined the Order of St. Janyl the Hermit in 1993. He receives anyone who comes on foot, blesses people and horses, listens and gives advice, and takes no money. He refuses to be filmed. A television crew that climbed to him in 2019 was sent back down with its camera unopened and a blessing.

His sayings travel. They circulate as stickers on the Tulpar app, and some are quoted in Talas as far as the Mejlis. The best known is the advice he is said to have given to a DPI deputy who climbed to see him: "Go back down and pay your drivers." The eparchy finds him awkward. He blesses pilgrims of the old faith and Muslim herders alike, and the Order protects him.

He agreed to speak to this newspaper on condition that nothing he said about anyone else was printed. Of himself he said little. "People climb because the city is loud," he said. "Up here it is quiet. That is all I give them. The quiet was here before me."

headline: Football without FIFA: Three Decades of the Irad League
dek: The federation founded in 1993 has built a league, a national team and two stadiums worth the name. What it has never had is a place in world football.
paragraphs: When the Football Federation of Irad was registered in 1993, its first act was a rule on names. Clubs had to take Iradi or neutral titles, and so Neftyanik became Neftchi Nurzhan, Dinamo Talas became Tulpar and the railway club Lokomotiv became Temirjolchu. The first Irad League season followed in 1994. Since then the league has missed only one season, 2007, cancelled because of the war.

The federation’s other project has gone nowhere. In 1996 it applied to the Asian Football Confederation, pointing to the membership of other US territories such as Guam. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan objected, and the application was deferred without a decision. A new application in 2008 was not taken up, because FIFA requires its members to represent a recognized state. Federation president Kanat Ermekov, a former Tulpar defender, calls the 1996 deferral “the theft of a generation”.

Without official internationals, the national team, in white and crimson at the Silk Road Arena, plays friendlies against Iradi American selections from Chicago, Kazakh club sides and teams of US service personnel, along with the Irad Day friendly first played in 1995. Since 2014 the federation has belonged to CONIFA, and the team played in its World Football Cup in 2016 and 2018. Players who want official international football must take the citizenship of a neighbor, as Iradi wrestlers have done.

headline: Journalist's accreditation restored
dek: Aigul Daniyar, whose press accreditation was withdrawn in 2020 after a report on arsenic in wells near the Chatkal smelter, can again work as an accredited reporter.
paragraphs: The press accreditation of Aigul Daniyar, an investigative journalist who reports on pollution and safety in the mining industry, has been restored, she said yesterday. The ISEZ withdrew it in 2020 after she published a report on arsenic levels in wells near the Chatkal smelter.

Daniyar has written for the Steppe Investigative Network since 2014. She has reported on seepage from the Chatkal Tailings Repository, on dust at the Sary-Bulak Antimony Works and on the Soviet uranium tailings at Mailuu-Suu. The companies concerned disputed her 2020 report on the wells, which lie near the smelter of the Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex in Sary-Bulak District.
"I am glad to have my card back. I would rather have had answers about the water," Daniyar told the Herald. She said she had been given no reason for the withdrawal or for the decision to reverse it.

The Department of Public Information confirmed that her accreditation had been renewed following a review and said it did not comment on individual cases. The Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine, which controls the smelter, has said that it monitors emissions and water in line with ISEZ regulations.

headline: Concrete in the Kucheh: Can the Old City Survive Its Own Success?
dek: Tourism has brought money to the lanes around the citadel. It has also brought cranes, concrete and hotels to the edge of the protected zone.
paragraphs: Walk down any lane (kucheh) in the Old City on a summer evening and the quarter seems to be thriving. The teahouses are full, saddlers and komuz makers are working with their doors open, and guesthouses advertise rooms in three languages. Tourism has become the main source of income for many of the families who live in the lanes around the old Kokand citadel.

Look up, though, and the cranes are visible. The Historic Districts Ordinance adopted by the city council in 1997 protects a zone of about 64 hectares around the citadel, bars the demolition of listed buildings and limits new construction to two stories. Since 2007, permits have been granted for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the zone, and inside it a number of mudbrick courtyard houses with carved walnut porches have been replaced by concrete buildings. Outside the zone the law offers little protection. In 2018 a merchant house of 1910 near Bazar-i Kalan was demolished to make way for a hotel.

The city government says that all new projects comply with the ordinance. Architects and residents who spoke to the Herald said that compliance with the letter of the ordinance was not the same as protecting the quarter. "Two stories of concrete is still concrete," said one architect who took part in last year's successful campaign to list the Philharmonic Hall.

The quarter has no international safety net. Because Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, the citadel quarter cannot be nominated for the World Heritage List, whatever its merits.

headline: Thirty years on, the steppe remembers Kudaibergen
dek: At the memorial cairn on the railway approaches to Nurzhan, Sabyrbek Duishön uulu spoke yesterday for his brother, thirty years after the battle at the Kobozev railhead.
paragraphs: On a low rise beside the railway approaches to Nurzhan, where a cairn of steppe stones marks the place Kudaibergen Duishön uulu fell, several hundred people gathered yesterday to mark thirty years since the battle of the Kobozev railhead. Riders came from the Boztorgoy camps, families came by bus from Talas, and Nurzhan schoolchildren from the school that bears his name brought flowers.

Kudaibergen is one of the few figures of the 1992 war honoured on both sides of the Qara-Chik line. Popular legend credits him with breaking the socialist counterattack at the railhead, and steppe bards sang *koshok* laments for him yesterday as they have every 28 July since. Military historians, and the documentary history published by Talas State University, give the decisive role to American air strikes, and the number of tanks destroyed by Iradi fighters has never been confirmed. Nobody at the cairn mentioned the dispute.

His brother Sabyrbek, the Boztorgoy *biy*, spoke for about ten minutes. "My brother did not ride for the steppe or for the city," he said. "He rode for the people behind him. Thirty years on, they are still behind him, and some of them are in this city."
Afterwards an old rider who fought in the battle sat on the cairn's lowest stones with his grandson. "The historians are right about the aeroplanes," he said. "But the aeroplanes did not have names."

headline: Bean growers count the cost of a dry summer
dek: Rotation schedules on the lower Talas canals have left bean fields in Kara-Buura short of water at flowering time, and growers blame the Agricultural Directorate.
paragraphs: In the lower Talas valley, July is when the bean fields need water most, and this year many of them did not get enough. Growers in Kara-Buura District say that rotation schedules imposed on the main canals in the hottest weeks of the summer left their plants short of water at flowering, and that they expect lower yields of the crop that has become the valley's best-known export.

Under the schedules, set by the Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate, canals are opened to each area in turn. Growers at the tail of the system said their turns had come too late and too briefly. "By the time the water reaches us, the big farms upstream have had their fill," said Nazgul Toktomusheva, who grows beans for export on 12 hectares outside Kyzyl-Adyr. Most of the valley's beans are sold to Turkey.

Farmers' associations have long criticized the directorate for slow canal repairs and for favoring large commercial farms when water is scarce. Several growers said that leaks from unlined canals in the lower valley, where waterlogging and salinity are already a problem, had made matters worse this year.

The directorate said the rotations had been applied equally across the valley and that its staff were inspecting the canals in Kara-Buura. It said that certified seed and fertilizer would continue to be sold at subsidized prices for the autumn. Its budget, which depends on allocations from the ISEZ, is not published in detail.

headline: No horns, please: Altyn Muuz on the road
dek: On a summer tour of district towns, the novelty boy band found venues unwilling to book four young men in bull horns, and switched to golden argali horns.
paragraphs: The four members of Altyn Muuz took the stage of the district club in Kyzyl-Adyr on Saturday night in sequined quilted coats and golden horns. The horns were not the ones their fans know. Instead of the bull horns of their videos, they wore the curling horns of the argali, the wild mountain sheep.

The change came early in the group's summer tour of district towns, when several venues declined to book it. Older villagers still repeat the grandmother's saying that cattle bring bad luck, and the church objects to anything that recalls Morkhan, the bull-headed god it identifies with Satan. "In Talas the horns are a joke," said Nurbek Asanov. "In the villages, a bull on your head is not a joke. So we became sheep."

Altyn Muuz was formed in 2019 from the top four contestants of Jyldyz Jolu, the talent show on IradOne's youth channel. Its singles, "Kymyz Kymyz", "Morkhan Baby" and this year's "Zhylky Love", have made it a staple of weddings and children's parties. In 2021 its performance of "Morkhan Baby" on a Sunday-morning children's program drew complaints from clergy, and later broadcasts of the episode left the song out.
In Kyzyl-Adyr the hall was full of families, and a row of students at the back wore homemade cardboard horns. Most of them, too, had switched to argali.

headline: Fifteen years on, the mothers come back to Qara-Chik
dek: On the anniversary of the 2007 ceasefire, the mothers of the missing stood at the checkpoint again with their sons' photographs.
paragraphs: About sixty women stood at the Qara-Chik checkpoint yesterday morning, on the fifteenth anniversary of the Bishkek ceasefire, holding photographs of sons who went missing in the war of 2007. Most were from the villages of Kara-Buura District. They have come every 12 September since the ceasefire.

Some of the photographs are faded school portraits. Others are laminated, and a few now carry a small black ribbon: since 2012 the Missing Persons Commission, which meets at Kara-Oi, has been finding graves, and the International Committee of the Red Cross has matched remains against the DNA samples given by families on both sides of the line. The first grave, of eleven men in a ravine above Merke, was found ten years ago.
"When they find him, I will come with the ribbon," said a woman of 71 from a Kara-Buura village, whose son was 19 in 2007. "Until then I come without it."

Gendarmerie officers at the checkpoint brought the women tea, as they do every year. Mothers from the tribal side, who have their own missing, stood at the other end of the crossing. At ten o'clock both groups stood in silence for a minute, and then went home.

headline: Nurzhan families wait for word from sons in Russia
dek: Since Russia’s mobilization order, young men with Russian passports have been coming home or sending their families ahead, and recruiters are calling on migrants.
paragraphs: Since Russia announced its partial mobilization last month, young men of Iradi origin who hold Russian citizenship have been returning to Nurzhan, or sending their wives and children there, according to families, the bus stations and the Irad Fellow-Countrymen’s Association in Moscow.

Tatyana Gorbunova’s son, who studied in Yekaterinburg and took Russian citizenship after graduating, put his wife and daughter on a bus to Nurzhan two weeks ago and has stayed behind for his job. “He calls every night,” she said. “I don’t sleep until he does.”

Migrants working in Russia on Kyrgyz and Kazakh passports, who are not liable to mobilization, report being approached by recruiters offering contract military service. The Department of Public Information has advised ISEZ residents working in Russia not to sign any military contract.

The fellow-countrymen’s association, which gives migrants legal advice, said its telephone lines had been busy since the order. An estimated 70,000 to 120,000 ISEZ residents work in Russia at the peak of the season, most of them Russian-speaking men from Nurzhan and Talas.

headline: Stolen for the knife: where Iradi horses go
dek: Horse theft carries up to fifteen years in the ISEZ and a ninefold fine on the tribal side. Police say most stolen horses still end up across the Kazakh frontier.
paragraphs: Ermek Jumagulov found the gate of his paddock open on a September morning and the hoofprints of his three geldings heading north. “They were not racehorses,” he said. “They were the horses my sons ride. Somebody wanted them for meat.”

Police say most horses stolen in the ISEZ are driven across the frontier into Kazakhstan, where horsemeat is a festive food, and that some go directly to slaughterhouses there. Commercial horse slaughter has been banned in Irad since 1996, and among Iradis eating horsemeat carries a stigma that ethnographers compare with eating dog in the West.

Since a 2009 amendment to the Criminal Code, horse theft has been an aggravated offense in the ISEZ, punishable by three to ten years in prison, and by up to fifteen where the horse is registered breeding stock or is stolen for slaughter. On the tribal side, customary law requires the thief’s kin to return the horse and pay nine animals for one, and a repeat thief may be expelled from his clan. Theft for slaughter is counted the worst of all.
District police say they recover few horses once they have crossed the frontier.

headline: Naryn schedule renewed for five years after four months of talks
dek: The joint technical commission formally adopts the Toktogul framework schedule to 2027, after a summer of deadlock over compensation for flooded pastures.
paragraphs: The joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol on Saturday formally adopted a renewed five-year framework schedule for releases from the Toktogul reservoir, at a meeting chaired by a UNMI official at the mission's sector headquarters in Tash-Kömür.

The schedule, which runs until 2027, divides the reservoir's stored water between winter generation and summer irrigation. Like the renewals of 2012 and 2017, it makes only minor changes to the framework first adopted in 2007, and it keeps the minimum reserve level introduced after the record low of 2008. This year's renewal followed four months of talks. Agreement in principle was reached in early September, after the tribal side's consent was settled at the Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau.

That consent was held up for much of the summer. Kökjal elders of the Toktogul basin, many of whose families were resettled when the reservoir was filled, refused to agree to further drawdown without compensation for flooded pastures. The deadlock was broken when three elders from outside the reservoir area, led by Biybolot Moldosh uulu, proposed that a fixed yearly share of the tribal side's Toktogul revenue go to a fund for Toktogul-basin families run by Kökjal elders. The Kökjal then stood aside.

Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attended the meeting without a vote. The Kyrgyz delegation filed its customary written reservation. The division of export revenue between the two administrations is set out in an annex that has never been published, and neither side commented on whether it had been changed.

headline: Our Almaz, their flag
dek: Almaz Samat uulu of Kara-Buura took another medal at the Asian championships this week, for Kazakhstan. Taraz is on his team card. Kara-Buura is on ours.
paragraphs: When Almaz Samat uulu stepped onto the podium this week with another medal at the Asian wrestling championships, IradOne Sport's caption named him as he has been named since 2019: "Almaz Samat uulu (Kara-Buura)". The flag raised behind him was Kazakhstan's, and the Kazakh team list gives his home as Taraz.

Mr. Samat uulu, 25, grew up in a village in Kara-Buura District and learned to wrestle at the district sports school. He took Kazakh citizenship four years ago, as Iradi wrestlers who want to compete at world level must: the Irad Olympic Committee, formed in 1993, has never been admitted by the International Olympic Committee, which recognises only committees of states recognised by the international community.

Each of his medals reopens the argument. Commentators close to the Democratic Party of Irad call athletes like him "borrowed flags" and say they lend weight to the neighbours' claims on Irad. The committee says they had no choice. His old coach in Kara-Buura, who asked not to be named, said the wrestler still trains at the district hall when he comes home in the summer. "Every boy in that hall wants to be Almaz," he said. "None of them asks which flag."
In the bazaar in Kara-Buura on Thursday the medal was the only subject. "Ours," said a melon seller. "Theirs on paper. Ours."

headline: Breeder jailed over Akyel pedigree fraud
dek: The owner of the Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud was sentenced to four years for substituting DNA samples for foals registered in the National Akyel Studbook.
paragraphs: The Talas District Court yesterday sentenced Kanat Ormonbekov, owner of the private Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud near Talas, to four years in prison for fraud and the forgery of veterinary documents.

The court found that Ormonbekov submitted samples from other horses in place of those of 14 foals registered between 2017 and 2021, with the help of Aizada Sydykbekova, a technician at the Talas Veterinary Research Center. Sydykbekova received a two-year suspended sentence.

The case came to light in March last year, when a retest commissioned by a US buyer showed that a palomino Akyel colt did not match its registered sire. The Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate, which keeps the studbook, struck 31 horses from it, and exports to the United States were suspended for four months.

Independent breeders who attended the hearings asked why the syndicate’s own farms had not been audited by an outside body. The syndicate’s managing director, Mirlan Toktarov, has said an internal review found nothing wrong at its farms. Ormonbekov’s lawyer said he would appeal.

headline: Fifty years on, the lakes are still watched
dek: Fifty years ago last night, a moraine lake above Kara-Buura burst and buried the village of Sary-Say. The men who watch the lakes now say it is why they are there.
paragraphs: On the night of 23 July 1973 a glacial lake on the north slope of the Talas Alatau burst through its moraine dam and sent a flood of mud and boulders down onto the village of Sary-Say above Kara-Buura. The official toll was 41. A list published in 1989 named about 300 dead. Last night, fifty years on, survivors and their families held a vigil where the village stood.

The disaster is the reason the Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service and the Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory now watch the moraine lakes of the range. Observers climb to the most dangerous of them each summer to measure their levels, and automatic gauges send readings to Talas.

"Every lake we watch, we watch because of Sary-Say," said a hydrologist at the monitoring service, who has climbed to the lakes above Kara-Buura for twenty years. "Never another Sary-Say. That is the whole of our job description." As the glaciers retreat, he said, new lakes form each decade, and the service now watches about thirty.

At the vigil an old man who was twelve in 1973 read the names from the 1989 list. It took more than an hour. Afterwards, he said, people in Kara-Buura still say they hear a bell from under the mud on hot July nights. "I do not hear it," he said. "But I understand why they do."

headline: Nurzhan textile plant cuts shifts as water runs short
dek: For the second time in three summers, Zhetysu Industrial Textiles has reduced working hours after the irrigation inspectorate cut its water quota.
paragraphs: Zhetysu Industrial Textiles, the Nurzhan wool and textile combine, has cut shifts at its scouring and dyeing sections after the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate reduced its summer water quota, the company said yesterday.

Scouring raw wool and dyeing yarn use large amounts of water, which the plant draws from the lower Chu basin. The company said reduced shifts would continue for several weeks, until the quota is restored or the river rises. Weaving and felt workshops are less affected. The plant employs about 1,100 people, most of them women.

It is the second time in three summers that the plant has had to cut back. It did the same in 2021, when quotas were reduced during the drought of that year. The company has asked for permission to drill its own wells, saying this would protect production in dry summers. The authorities have not approved the request. The company says its scouring lines already recycle most of their water.

The inspectorate said this summer's quotas had been set for all large users of the lower Chu according to the water available, and that no user had been treated differently. Workers leaving the morning shift yesterday said they had been told that wages for the lost hours would be partly paid. "We have been through this before," one weaver said. "We wait for the river."

headline: Film festival audiences fall again
dek: The Irad Film Society blames lost sponsorship and travel difficulties; critics point to a program still built around Russian-language cinema.
paragraphs: Admissions to last month's Talas International Film Festival fell again, and fewer foreign guests attended than at the last edition in 2021, the Irad Film Society said on Saturday.

The society did not publish a final count, but said admissions were well under half the 62,000 recorded in 2005, the festival's best year, when the restored Desert Sun's Rebellion opened the program. Several weekday screenings in the cinemas of Cinema Boulevard played to fewer than twenty people.

The society attributed the decline to reduced corporate sponsorship and to travel difficulties caused by Irad's unresolved international status, which it said had again deterred several invited guests from abroad. "Every festival we spend more of our time on visas and less on films," a member of the society's board said.

Critics point to the program instead. A large section of this year's festival was again given to Russian-language films from Russia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, at a time when younger audiences in Talas increasingly watch films in English and Iradi. Many of them now go to the Diz festival in the citadel courtyards each summer instead.

headline: Three Tickets Registered for Gubernatorial Ballot
dek: The Territorial Election Commission accepts three of five nominations for the November election; two are rejected on signature-verification grounds.
paragraphs: The Territorial Election Commission yesterday registered three tickets for the gubernatorial election on 7 November, and rejected two other nominations on signature-verification grounds under the procedures adopted in 2015.

Governor Erlan Toktarov of the Democratic Party of Irad, renominated by the party congress in Talas in August, will seek a fourth elected term with Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat as his running mate. He is opposed by Oleg Zubarev, an engineer and Nurzhan city councillor aligned with the city's Russian-speaking bloc, who is standing as an independent with a Nurzhan trade-union official as running mate, and by Damira Kenesbay, a Talas pediatrician known for her campaign on drinking-water quality in the city's outer districts.

The commission did not publish the names of the two rejected nominees. Under the 2015 procedures, nominations must be supported by verified signatures, and the commission said both had fallen short. Opposition lawyers say there is no effective appeal against the commission's decisions.

Two of the best-known critics of the government will not be on the ballot. Kamran Bekzatov, the president of NurGaz, has never stood for office and has not endorsed a candidate. The commentator Jason Ilyasov, a US citizen who settled in Talas in 2016, does not meet the Elective Governor Acts' requirement of ten years' residence and did not seek nomination. The official campaign opens this week.

headline: Students map the stairways of Chong-Say
dek: Volunteers from Talas State University are walking every stairway of the hillside quarter with notebooks and a GPS, because the official map stops at the last road.
paragraphs: Volunteers from Talas State University spent the weekend climbing the stairways of Chong-Say, one of the oldest hillside quarters of Iyık Janyl, with notebooks, tape measures and a GPS receiver, to draw the first map of the quarter that shows how its residents actually get home.

Kartalar, Attelkom's online map, shows only Chong-Say's main lanes, because its survey cars cannot enter them. Most addresses in the quarter are given by landmarks: the chapel, the blue water tank, the shop with the white door. Ambulance drivers say they find patients by asking.

The students, from the geography department, are numbering every stairway and footpath and marking standpipes, steps that flood in spring and the places where hoses and electricity cables cross. They hope to finish Chong-Say by the spring and give the map to the city, the ambulance service and Attelkom.

Residents brought them tea and corrected their names for the lanes. "This one is not the 'stairs by the tank'," a grandmother told them, pointing. "It is Yuhanna's stairs. Yuhanna built them in 1974." The students wrote it down.

headline: Students March on Government House
dek: Students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University to the government district to protest a new municipal licensing surcharge.
paragraphs: Students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University to Government House yesterday to protest a new municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers. The march appeared to have no formal organizers; participants said it had been arranged through messaging groups over the weekend.

The surcharge was announced by the Talas municipal administration this month. Criticism spread after the commentator Jason Ilyasov called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet" on IradOne's OneDebate, and clips of the exchange circulated widely on social media. Estimates of the crowd varied widely: the police put it at several hundred, while student groups said several thousand took part. Some small traders from the Bazar-i Kalan area joined the march.

Police lines blocked the approaches to Government House, and marchers sang the anthem and chanted slogans against the levy before dispersing in the evening. "I deliver food to pay for my studies. Now they want a license fee for my bicycle," said a third-year economics student who gave her name as Aizhan. The municipal administration said the surcharge was a lawful licensing measure and would apply as planned. Students said they would return today.

headline: Marchers sing the anthem as water cannon clear the government district
aliases: Talas Herald (2023; 2025). Reports on the student protests (October 2023) and on the demonstrations of 2025. Talas.
dek: Students and couriers protesting a new licensing surcharge sang “The Spirit of Irad” as police and Gendarmerie units broke up their march with tear gas and water cannon.
paragraphs: Several thousand students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University toward the government district yesterday afternoon to protest the municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers announced this month.

As police and units of the Republican Gendarmerie blocked the avenue, the front ranks stopped and sang the first stanza and refrain of “The Spirit of Irad”, most with their right hands over their hearts. Officers moved in with tear gas and water cannon minutes later. Marchers who regrouped in side streets sang the anthem again, along with songs by the Mor-Wave duo tüntolk.

Student groups said dozens were detained. The city police and the Gendarmerie did not give figures. Mobile data was unavailable in central Talas for much of the evening; Attelkom did not respond to questions.

The municipal administration has said the surcharge is needed to regulate a fast-growing sector. The protests began after the commentator Jason Ilyasov criticized the levy on IradOne’s OneDebate. Most participants interviewed by the Herald said they had come through messaging groups and belonged to no party.

headline: Church appeals for restraint on Central Square
dek: The Council of Hierarchs asks police and protesters alike to refrain from violence as students and couriers return to the city center.
paragraphs: The Council of Hierarchs of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, the assembly of its bishops, yesterday appealed to both the police and the protesters in Talas to show restraint, after a week of marches against the city's new licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers.

In a statement issued from Iyık Janyl in the name of the council, the bishops said that "no grievance is served by broken windows, and no order is served by broken heads". They asked parish priests in Talas to keep their churches open in the evenings for anyone in need of shelter or care, and called on the authorities to release detained minors to their families.

Police and Gendarmerie units used tear gas and water cannon on Thursday evening to clear students and couriers from Central Square, where they had gathered after marching from Talas State University. The Gendarmerie said a number of people had been detained for administrative offenses but gave no figure. The Legal Defense Guild said it was representing detained students. Mobile data has been unavailable in central Talas since Thursday. Attelkom has described the outage as technical work.
A spokesman for the Talas municipal administration said the surcharge had been lawfully adopted. The Department of Public Information did not comment on the bishops' statement.

headline: Mobile data restored in central Talas after three days
dek: Attelkom brought mobile internet back to the city center yesterday; its Director-General said the company had been legally bound to comply with a security directive.
paragraphs: Mobile data service returned to central Talas yesterday afternoon, three days after it was cut on Thursday evening as police and Gendarmerie units cleared students and couriers from Central Square.

Attelkom, the largest telecommunications company in the ISEZ, had described the outage as technical work. In a statement yesterday its Director-General, Samat Kasymov, said the company had acted on a directive from the security authorities. "Attelkom is legally bound to comply with security directives," the statement said. "Service was restored as soon as the directive was lifted." It did not say which authority had issued the order or why.

The cut affected mobile internet in the government district, around Talas State University and in the Old City. Voice calls and text messages largely continued to work, as did fixed-line connections. Delivery couriers, whose protest against the municipal licensing surcharge began the marches, said they had been unable to take orders, and traders near Bazar-i Kalan said card payments had failed. During the outage the Herald posted free PDF editions of its pages on a mirror site and sold printed copies on the street.

Rights groups criticized the shutdown. The Legal Defense Guild said it had made it harder for families to learn where detained relatives were being held. The Department of Public Information did not respond to questions.

headline: Degrees without jobs: the economics behind the student protests
dek: The courier levy lit the fuse, but the grievance underneath it is a labor market that has no place for the graduates Talas produces.
paragraphs: The marches that filled the government district this month began over a licensing surcharge on startups and couriers. It is worth asking why so many of the marchers were graduates, or about to become graduates, and why a fee on delivery bicycles touched them so closely.

Unemployment in the ISEZ is not reliably measured, which is itself part of the problem. But anyone who teaches at Talas State University knows where our graduates go. Foreign companies and the bases hire English speakers, which favors young urban Iradis, but those jobs are few. The public sector is full. Nurzhan's oil and industrial sector still recruits mainly among the Russian-speaking generation. What is left is the work young people make for themselves: delivery, small software firms, translation, online trade. The surcharge fell on exactly that.

A levy on the one part of the economy that absorbs underemployed graduates is a tax on a safety valve. The authorities have said the surcharge is a lawful licensing measure, and so it may be. The question is whether it is a wise one. Suspending it and opening the licensing rules for small firms to public consultation would cost the city little revenue and would show the students that someone in the administration has done the arithmetic they did.

headline: Security Council extends UN mission for another year
dek: The UN Security Council has renewed the mandate of the observer mission on the Qara-Chik line for twelve months.
paragraphs: The United Nations Security Council yesterday renewed the mandate of the United Nations Mission in Irad for a further twelve months, keeping the unarmed observer mission on the Qara-Chik line until October next year.

The mission, established in October 2007 after the Bishkek ceasefire, monitors the line, about 1,890 km long, between the ISEZ and the tribal regions, supervises the joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, and coordinates humanitarian aid and mine clearance on both sides of the line. It is headquartered at Kara-Oi. The council has renewed the mandate every October since 2008.

As in previous years, members differed over whether the resolution should refer to the unification referendum, the political status of the territory and the foreign military presence at Talas Air Base. The Secretary-General's latest report also noted that UNMI patrols have been barred this year from a security zone around the Boz-Korgon compound east of Nurzhan. The ISEZ government says the zone is an ordinary industrial and security area unconnected with the ceasefire. The Department of Public Information welcomed the renewal.

headline: Protesters move to Tulpar as foreign apps slow
dek: With mobile data cut in central Talas and foreign platforms throttled, students and couriers took their group chats to the home-grown app, which kept working.
paragraphs: As mobile data was cut in central Talas and several foreign social-media platforms slowed to a crawl across the ISEZ this week, students and couriers moved their group chats to Tulpar, the messaging app founded by the commentator Jason Ilyasov, which continued to work on home broadband and outside the city centre.

Tulpar said yesterday that more than 140,000 new accounts had been registered since Monday, roughly doubling its users. Several of the largest protest channels, including one for delivery couriers with 31,000 members, now run on the app. Attelkom, which described the outage in central Talas as "technical work", did not say why Tulpar was unaffected.

The municipal licensing surcharge that set off the protests applies to independent technology startups as well as couriers, among them Tulpar Technologies itself. Mr. Ilyasov, who was released from administrative detention on Thursday, said the app "is not a party, it is a pipe" and that it did not moderate political channels.

A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the government was "aware of the use of certain applications to organise unauthorised gatherings" and would review "the responsibilities of their owners". He declined to name the app.

headline: Licensing Surcharge Suspended after Student Protests
dek: The Lieutenant Governor has suspended the municipal levy on startups and couriers that set off last month's marches in Talas.
paragraphs: Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat yesterday announced the suspension of the municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers whose introduction last month set off student and courier protests in Talas.

Speaking at a meeting with business representatives in Talas, Maksat said the decision followed a review of the levy by the governorate and the municipal administration, which had concluded that it placed "a disproportionate burden on small and new enterprises". He said the licensing rules for small firms would be revised in consultation with business groups. Couriers already charged would not have to pay outstanding amounts while the suspension lasts, a municipal official said.

The announcement comes days before Tuesday's general election, in which Maksat is again Governor Erlan Toktarov's running mate on the DPI ticket. Opposition commentators described the timing as electoral; the government said the decision was the result of the review. Student groups welcomed the suspension but said they would continue to press for the release of those still held after the October protests.

headline: Semiz sends first Mexican-Iradi to city council
dek: Andrés Ochoa Kaparov, 23, son of a SuKarne veterinarian and an Iradi teacher, won a seat for western Talas on the DPI list.
paragraphs: Andrés Ochoa Kaparov has become the first Mexican-Iradi member of the Talas city council, elected on Tuesday on the list of the Democratic Party of Irad for the western Talas constituency, which includes Semiz.

Ochoa Kaparov, 23, was born in Talas in 2000 to a SuKarne veterinarian from Culiacán and an Iradi teacher, and worked as an interpreter at the plant before entering politics. He speaks Spanish, Iradi and English. At the count he thanked “both my families, the one in the blocks and the one in the courtyards”.

Because his mother is Iradi, he is registered as an ISEZ resident and can vote and stand. Mexican-born residents of the district, who hold residence permits, cannot vote, and several told the Herald they had followed the campaign without taking part.

Critics described the nomination as a DPI gesture toward the western corridor. The party said he had been chosen on merit. The community of more than 10,000 Mexicans in Talas, the largest in Central Asia, grew from the staff of the SuKarne and Conagra plants, which opened during the territorial period.

headline: Courier Levy Sparked Student Marches, Now Suspended
dek: How a municipal surcharge on startups and couriers led to the largest protests in Talas in years, and how it ended.
paragraphs: In early October the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. On OneDebate, IradOne's prime-time panel, the commentator Jason Ilyasov called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet", and clips of the exchange spread widely. Within days students and couriers gathered at Talas State University and marched on the government district. Most observers described the protests as spontaneous and leaderless. The authorities said Ilyasov had instigated them, citing a speech on the third day in which he urged protesters not to pay the levy.

Police and Gendarmerie units under Major General Ruslan Toktarov dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Ruslan Toktarov described the organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". Mobile data was cut in central Talas for three days; Attelkom called the outage "technical work". Ilyasov was held for three days and released without charge after press-freedom groups criticized his detention. A Herald reporter, Erkin Bolot uulu, was held for ten days for "obstructing police" while photographing a march, and was released without charge.

On 3 November, four days before the election, Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat announced that the surcharge would be suspended. The Legal Defense Guild of Gulnara Sadyk says it is representing more than sixty detained students. Human Rights Watch has criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.

headline: IradOne drops tüntolk videos after protests
aliases: Talas Herald (2023). Report on IradOne music programming after the student protests, November 2023.
Talas Herald (2019; 2023). Reports on ... IradOne music programming (November 2023) [the 2023 half of the combined citation]
dek: Videos from the duo's 2017 album have disappeared from rotation on IradOne's youth channel since songs from it were sung at last month's marches.
paragraphs: Several music videos by the Mor-Wave duo tüntolk have been removed from rotation on IradOne since songs from their album White Stallion in Fog were sung by students at the October protests in Talas, according to the broadcaster's published schedules and to presenters at the channel.

The videos, which IradOne itself commissioned after the album's release in 2017, show Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage lines in the Moiynkum steppe. They had been among the most frequently shown on the youth channel. None has appeared in the published music schedules since late October. Two presenters, who asked not to be named, said they had been told not to request them. Videos by other Mor-Wave and Mor-Pop acts continue to be shown.
IradOne did not respond to written questions from the Herald. The Department of Public Information said programming decisions were a matter for the broadcaster.

Asked about the change, the duo said only that their songs "belong to whoever sings them". The protests began last month over a municipal licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers and were dispersed by police and Gendarmerie units. Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat announced this month that the surcharge would be suspended.

headline: Six checkpoint sergeants jailed for tanker bribes
dek: The Talas District Court convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to wave fuel tankers through the main crossing on the Qara-Chik line. No officer above them was charged.
paragraphs: Six sergeants of the Republican Gendarmerie were sentenced to prison yesterday after the Talas District Court convicted them of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint on the Qara-Chik line, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley.

The prosecution said the tankers carried diesel under false manifests and were bound for the tribal regions, where the UN mission reported this year that diesel sells in Chatkal valley villages for 40 to 60 percent more than in Talas. The court heard that payments were made in cash at the barrier and passed between the men on shift.

In a statement after the verdict, the Gendarmerie said the case showed that its internal discipline worked and that “no uniform protects a thief”. No officer above the rank of sergeant was charged, and the prosecution did not say whether its inquiry had examined who supervised the shifts.

Exile outlets and FreeIrad.org have alleged that senior Gendarmerie figures take part in the fuel trade into the tribal regions. The allegations are unverified. The Gendarmerie has denied them, and no inquiry has been opened.

headline: Why we don't print what we can't check
aliases: Why we don’t print what we can’t check
dek: Readers ask why this newspaper does not report what FreeIrad.org says. The answer is in the word "report".
paragraphs: Since the student protests last month, a good number of readers have written to ask why the Herald does not report the claims of FreeIrad.org, whose posters have appeared at demonstrations and whose slogans our readers' children repeat. Some letters accuse us of cowardice. Others accuse us of being paid. Neither is the reason.

A newspaper reports what it can check: a document it has seen, a person who will speak, a court file, a figure in a budget. FreeIrad's exposés rest on unnamed sources, and most of what it publishes can be traced to the same chat groups our readers already read. Repeating a rumour in print does not make it a fact. It only makes it a rumour with our name on it.

This is not a judgment on the anger that brings people to the site. Much of that anger is about real things: the price of bread, the data cuts, the Governor's absence from the questions young people ask. When those things can be documented, we document them, and we will go on doing so whether or not the Department of Public Information approves.

We will report FreeIrad when FreeIrad is the news: when it is blocked, when its claims are tested in a court, or when someone is harmed by what it says. Until then readers who want rumour know where to find it. We would rather they found something else here.

headline: Betting site behind Jarysh odds page blocked
dek: Attelkom has blocked bet.jarysh.com at the Directorate's request. Jarysh says its odds are "for information and entertainment only".
paragraphs: Attelkom has blocked access to bet.jarysh.com, a betting site run for the Curaçao-registered company Steppe Gaming N.V., after the National Equestrian Sports Directorate asked for it to be added to the list of restricted resources under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011.

The address had been linked from the "Jarysh Odds" page of jarysh.com, which publishes odds on ulak league matches. Under the act, wagers may be placed only at the Directorate's licensed tote windows.

Jarysh Entertainment Group said it did not take bets and that Steppe Gaming was "only an advertiser". Its odds page remains open. Bookmakers told the Herald that bets were now being taken through channels on the Tulpar messaging app.

headline: Third frozen death of the winter on the Chu road
dek: A 47-year-old man was found dead on the verge of the Chu road near Nurzhan on Saturday morning, after walking home from a wedding. It is the third such death this winter.
paragraphs: A 47-year-old man from a village on the Chu road was found dead of cold on the verge about four kilometres from his home early on Saturday, the Nurzhan district police said. He had left a wedding in a neighbouring village on foot shortly after midnight, when the temperature was minus 24.

Police said the man had been drinking and appeared to have sat down to rest. It is the third death of its kind on the Chu road and its villages this winter, after a man of 52 in December and a man of 38 earlier this month. Relatives found him after he failed to come home.

Doctors at the Nurzhan district hospital said deaths of men walking home drunk in winter were "a tradition nobody wants". The district administration said it would ask village heads to keep a car at every wedding for guests who live along the road, as some villages already do.
"Everyone knows the rule: if you drink, you sleep where you drank," said a village head near Chu. "Everyone also knows that nobody keeps it."

headline: An American detective series makes a Talas teahouse band famous
dek: Eski Ün's "Dream of Living", a Mor-Folk song recorded in a borrowed boiler room, has been heard by millions since it played on True Detective.
paragraphs: Five years ago Eski Ün could not get a concert past the parish priests of Iyık Janyl.
